scripts.name: Chinese characters (Hanzi)
scripts.sample: 大明宣德年製 開元通寶
scripts.sampleMeaning: 'Made in the Xuande reign of the Great Ming' (a porcelain reign mark) + 'Kaiyuan tongbao' (the standard Tang coin legend)
look: Square, self-contained characters of equal size, each built from several strokes inside an invisible box
Traditionally in vertical columns read top to bottom, columns running right to left
No alphabet-like repetition: hundreds of different shapes, no word spaces
Often paired with red square seal impressions on paintings and calligraphy
Reign marks on ceramics are 4 or 6 characters in a double ring or square, usually ending 年製 'made in the years of'
scripts.onWhat: Oracle bones, ritual bronzes, coins (round with square hole), seals, stelae, porcelain bases, lacquer, jade, paintings and hand scrolls, sutras, printed books, textiles.
scripts.infer: Places the object in the Chinese cultural sphere, but not automatically in China: Korea, Japan and Vietnam all wrote in Chinese characters. The script style and the object type do the dating: uneven pictographic bronze script is Shang or Zhou, squat clerical script is Han, and flowing brush hands on paper or silk are 4th century onward. A reign mark gives a claimed emperor (many are later tributes). Kana mixed in means Japan; Hangul mixed in means Korea.

confusables.how: Japanese text mixes the square characters with simple curvy kana (の, し, を); pure-character text on a Japanese object cannot be told apart by script alone.
Hangul blocks are made of a few geometric parts (circles, straight bars) that repeat constantly; Korean objects before 1900 mostly use Chinese characters anyway.
Tangut looks Chinese at a distance but every character is unreadable, denser, and full of repeated diagonal strokes.
Chữ Nôm mixes ordinary Chinese characters with unfamiliar, heavier compounds invented for Vietnamese words.
'Phags-pa on Yuan coins and seals is squared and vertical like seal script but made of a small set of repeating alphabet letters.

styles.name: Oracle-bone and bronze script (jiǎgǔwén, jīnwén)
styles.where: Shang and Zhou: Anyang oracle bones, cast inscriptions inside ritual bronzes
styles.look: Pictographic and irregular: characters of unequal size, visible animals, hands, eyes; thin scratched lines on bone, rounded swelling lines when cast in bronze. No web font renders this.

styles.name: Seal script (zhuànshū)
styles.where: Warring States and Qin inscriptions, Qin-Han coins and weights; afterwards seals, stele titles and archaising inscriptions of every later period
styles.look: Even-width curving lines with no thick-thin contrast, tall symmetric forms, rounded corners. On a seal it tells you little about date; as the main text of an object it suggests Qin or earlier. No web font on Google Fonts.

styles.name: Clerical script (lìshū)
styles.where: Han dynasty stelae, bamboo and wooden slips, mirrors; revived by Qing calligraphers
styles.look: Squat, wide characters with flaring 'silkworm head, wild-goose tail' horizontal strokes. No web font on Google Fonts.

styles.name: Regular script (kǎishū)
styles.where: Standard from the Tang onward: stelae, sutras, reign marks, coin legends
styles.look: Upright, clearly separated strokes with brush-shaped ends, each stroke lifted. Sample reads 'peace under heaven'. This web font is a modern brush kaishu, a fair approximation.

styles.name: Printed Song/Ming typeface (sòngtǐ)
styles.where: Woodblock-printed books, later banknotes and printed labels
styles.look: Thin horizontals, thick verticals, small triangles at stroke ends: the look of woodblock printing, so Song or later.

styles.name: Running script (xíngshū)
styles.where: Letters, colophons on paintings, poems on scrolls and fans
styles.look: Regular-script shapes written fast: strokes link, corners round off, characters lean. The web font is a modern approximation.

styles.name: Cursive script (cǎoshū)
styles.where: Calligraphy scrolls, especially Tang, Song, Ming and Qing literati work
styles.look: Characters collapse into a few sweeping loops, often joined down the column; nearly illegible without training. The web font is a modern approximation.

scripts.name: Arabic: Kufic (angular) styles
scripts.sampleMeaning: 'Blessing to its owner' (baraka li-ṣāḥibihi), the stock good-wish inscription on early Islamic ceramics and metalwork
look: Angular and geometric: a strong flat baseline with straight verticals rising at right angles
Letters stretched horizontally, wide gaps, few or no dots; early Qur'ans mark vowels with red dots
On Qur'an leaves: horizontal-format parchment pages with only a few lines of thick dark-brown script
Later versions sprout leaves (foliated), flowers (floriated) or knots in the tall strokes
The web font here is a modern, simplified Kufic; historical Kufic is heavier and more stretched
scripts.onWhat: Early Qur'an leaves on parchment, coins (dinars and dirhams, entirely epigraphic), tiraz textile bands, slip-painted bowls, lustreware, carved wood and ivory, tombstones, architectural friezes.
scripts.infer: Kufic as the main script points to roughly 650-1200. Purely epigraphic gold and silver coins are Umayyad or Abbasid (after 696). Black Kufic on a white slip bowl is Samanid Nishapur or Samarkand, 10th century. Foliated Kufic on textiles, rock crystal or lustre is Fatimid Egypt (10th-12th century). After 1200 Kufic survives only for headings and architecture, with cursive carrying the main text.

confusables.how: Naskh and thuluth are rounded and flowing with full dots; Kufic is ruled, right-angled and sparse.
Maghribi keeps some Kufic stiffness but has deep swooping bowls below the line and is found on later western manuscripts.
Estrangela Syriac is also blocky and right-to-left but has no tall parallel verticals; letters are short and boxy with a dot-and-bar texture.
Arab-Sasanian coins carry a Sasanian king's bust with short Kufic words in the margin next to Pahlavi; pure Islamic coins have no image.

styles.name: Early Abbasid Kufic
styles.where: Qur'an leaves on parchment, Syria, Iraq, Egypt, North Africa
styles.look: Thick, horizontally stretched letters on a wide page, three to nine lines; red and green vowel dots; gold verse markers. No web font matches.

styles.name: Eastern Kufic ('New Style', broken cursive)
styles.where: Iran and Central Asia: Qur'ans on paper, Samanid epigraphic pottery
styles.look: Tall, slender verticals with sharp diagonal breaks and thin-to-thick contrast; triangular letter heads. Signals Iran or Khurasan, 10th-12th century. No web font matches.

styles.name: Foliated and floriated Kufic
styles.where: Fatimid Egypt, also Iran and Anatolia: tiraz, tombstones, woodwork
styles.look: Letter ends split into half-palmettes and tendrils; floral scrolls fill the upper band.

styles.name: Square Kufic (bannā'ī)
styles.where: Brick and tile architecture of Iran and Central Asia (Ilkhanid, Timurid, Safavid); Mamluk Cairo; continues in architecture after 1500
styles.look: Words turned into a maze-like square grid, often repeating Allah, Muhammad, Ali.

styles.name: Pseudo-Kufic
styles.where: Byzantine churches, Italian and Spanish textiles, Renaissance painting haloes
styles.look: Kufic-looking strokes that spell nothing: a decorative imitation, so the object is from the Christian Mediterranean.

scripts.name: Arabic: cursive styles (naskh, thuluth, muhaqqaq)
scripts.sampleMeaning: 'In the name of God, the Merciful, the Compassionate' (the basmala)
look: Rounded, flowing, joined letters written right to left, with dots above and below
Naskh: small, even, legible book hand with short verticals
Thuluth: large, with very tall verticals, sweeping curves and letters stacked and interlaced, used for display
Small vowel marks and decorative fillers float between the letters
Long words swell and thin with the reed pen: thick downstrokes, hairline joins
scripts.onWhat: Qur'ans and books on paper, inlaid brass and bronze (basins, candlesticks, pen boxes), enamelled glass mosque lamps, tiles, carpets and textiles, tombstones, coins after about 1200, mihrabs.
scripts.infer: Cursive as the main script means after about 1000. Bold thuluth bands with titles such as 'the high authority, the lord' on brass inlaid with silver or on enamelled glass are Mamluk Egypt or Syria (1250-1517). Small naskh in lustre tile borders is Kashan, Iran, 13th-14th century. Naskh alone does not separate regions: use the companion scripts (nasta'liq means Iran or India, a tughra means Ottoman) and the object type.

confusables.how: Kufic is angular with a ruled baseline; these hands are rounded and dotted.
Nasta'liq words slide diagonally down toward the left and look 'hanging'; naskh sits level on the line.
Maghribi has huge open bowls below the line and dots fa with one dot below, qaf with one dot above.
Divani is a dense chancery hand whose lines climb to the left, with letters knotted together and no spaces.
Serto Syriac is also cursive and right-to-left but is smaller, lower and lacks the tall alif-lam verticals.

styles.name: Naskh
styles.where: Book hand everywhere from Spain to India; small inscriptions on tiles and metalwork
styles.look: Compact, clear, level; the default copying hand after Ibn Muqla and Ibn al-Bawwab (10th-11th century).

styles.name: Thuluth
styles.where: Monumental and display script: Mamluk metalwork and glass, mosque lamps, Qur'an headings, architecture, Ottoman panels
styles.look: Sample reads 'Glory to our lord the sultan', the standard Mamluk formula. Tall uprights, deep curves, words overlapping in two tiers. No true thuluth web font on Google Fonts; a naskh font only hints at it.

styles.name: Muhaqqaq and rayhani
styles.where: Large Qur'ans of Mamluk Egypt, Ilkhanid and Timurid Iran
styles.look: Very large, shallow, sharply pointed sub-line strokes that sweep left; few lines per page. Big-format Qur'an leaves in this hand are 14th-15th century.

styles.name: Bihari
styles.where: Qur'ans of Sultanate India
styles.look: Wedge-shaped, thick horizontal strokes with widely spaced words, often in alternating colours: a strong pre-Mughal India signal.

styles.name: Sini (Chinese Arabic)
styles.where: Chinese Muslim bronzes, porcelain and mosque panels
styles.look: Arabic written with a soft brush, thick tapering strokes like Chinese calligraphy; often on Ming Zhengde blue-and-white.

scripts.name: Persian nasta'liq (with ta'liq and shikasta)
scripts.sampleMeaning: 'Abbas, servant of the King of Sanctity [Ali]', the formula of Shah Abbas I on seals and dedications
look: Each word hangs diagonally, starting high on the right and sliding down to the left
Very short verticals, long sweeping horizontal curves, strong thick-thin contrast
Usually in short poetic lines set in columns or cloud-shaped panels, often on gold-flecked or marbled paper
Album pages (muraqqa') show a few large lines set diagonally with illuminated corner pieces
Shikasta ('broken') is a faster, denser version that joins letters normally left separate
scripts.onWhat: Poetry manuscripts (Shahnama, Khamsa, Divan of Hafiz), album calligraphy, miniature-painting captions, Safavid and Mughal coins, seals, carpets with verse cartouches, jade and metalwork with poetry, tiles.
scripts.infer: Nasta'liq grew out of the ta'liq chancery hand and was perfected in Iran around 1400, so it gives a floor of about 1400 and points to the Persianate world: Timurid Herat, Safavid Iran, Uzbek Bukhara, Mughal and Deccan India, and Ottoman poetry. It is not used for Arabic-language Qur'an text. To choose between Iran and India use the painting style, borders and object type; Urdu and lithographed pages are 19th century.

confusables.how: Naskh sits level and upright; nasta'liq slopes down to the left and has almost no tall verticals.
Divani lines climb upward at the left end and are tightly knotted; nasta'liq words descend and are airy.
Maghribi is a western Qur'an and book hand with round bowls; it never hangs diagonally.

styles.name: Nasta'liq
styles.where: Iran, Central Asia, India
styles.look: The classic hanging hand; this web font is a faithful modern nasta'liq.

styles.name: Ta'liq
styles.where: Persian chancery documents
styles.look: Predecessor of nasta'liq: looping, with extra joins and lines that rise at the end.

styles.name: Shikasta
styles.where: Iranian and Indian letters, documents and late album pages
styles.look: Dense, tangled and rapid; letters fused, lines often written at angles and in margins. Later Safavid, Zand, Qajar or Mughal.

scripts.name: Latin alphabet
scripts.sampleMeaning: 'The Senate and People of Rome' (SPQR)
look: The familiar ABC; the question is which letterform family
Roman inscriptions: capitals only, V for U, no J or W, dots between words, heavy abbreviation (IMP CAES AVG, COS, D M)
Early medieval: rounded uncial or half-uncial letters, often with interlace initials
Gothic: tall, narrow, broken strokes packed into a dark picket-fence texture
Renaissance onward: clear roman and italic letters close to modern print
scripts.onWhat: Roman coins, stone inscriptions, lead pipes, brick stamps, military diplomas; medieval manuscripts, seals, reliquaries, enamels, tomb slabs, bells; later prints, medals, silver hallmarks, clock dials, firearms, scientific instruments.
scripts.infer: The letterform dates the object. Square capitals with V for U and imperial titles are Roman (roughly 100 BCE-400 CE); uncial is about 300-800; Carolingian minuscule 800-1200; Gothic blackletter 1150-1500 (and in German lands to the 1900s); humanist roman and italic after 1450; copperplate script 1650-1900. The language narrows place: French, German, English, Spanish or Dutch words on a post-medieval object beat any other clue.

confusables.how: Greek shares A B E K M N O T but shows Σ, Π, Δ, Λ, Φ, Ω; Roman-era Greek coins of the East look Latin until you spot these.
Etruscan runs right to left with mirrored letters and has no B, D or O.
Cyrillic mixes Latin-looking letters with Д, Ж, И, Ш, Я.
Runes are all straight strokes with no curves or horizontals; Latin capitals have round bowls.
Coptic looks like Greek uncial plus a few extra letters; it is not Latin.

styles.name: Roman square capitals
styles.where: Roman empire: stone, bronze, coin legends
styles.look: Stately capitals with thick-thin stress and serifs, V for U, interpuncts. Sample is the title of Augustus as it appears on coins.

styles.name: Rustic capitals
styles.where: Painted notices at Pompeii, early manuscripts, later only for headings
styles.look: Tall, narrow, slanted capitals with thin verticals and thick feet.

styles.name: Uncial, half-uncial and Insular
styles.where: Late antique and early medieval Gospel books; Ireland and Britain kept the Insular form to about 1100
styles.look: Rounded letters: curved d, e, m, single-compartment a; Insular pages add interlace and red dots. The web font is a modern display uncial.

styles.name: Carolingian minuscule
styles.where: Frankish empire and its successors; Ottonian and Romanesque manuscripts
styles.look: Round, clear, well-spaced lower-case with few ligatures, the ancestor of modern print. No dedicated web font; looks like a hand-written roman type.

styles.name: Gothic blackletter (textura, Fraktur)
styles.where: Psalters, books of hours, tomb brasses, seals, early printing; Fraktur stays in German-speaking lands to about 1940
styles.look: Dense, vertical, angular; letters fused, diamond-shaped feet. The web font is a 16th-century German Fraktur, rounder than medieval textura.

styles.name: Humanist roman and italic
styles.where: Italian Renaissance manuscripts and medals, then printing everywhere
styles.look: Clear open letters modelled on Carolingian minuscule; revived Roman capitals on medals and architecture. Sample is the opening of the Aeneid.

styles.name: Copperplate / round hand
styles.where: Engraved silver, trade cards, maps, samplers, letters
styles.look: Slanted, looping, hairline-and-swell pen script; typical of 18th-19th century Britain, America and France.

scripts.name: Greek alphabet
scripts.sampleMeaning: '[Coin] of King Alexander' (genitive coin legend)
look: Capitals with Σ, Π, Δ, Λ, Φ, Ψ, Ω, Θ, Ξ among Latin-looking A, B, E, K, M, N, O, T
Coin legends in the genitive: words ending -ΟΥ, -ΩΝ, -ΕΩΣ around a head or figure
Archaic inscriptions may run right to left or back and forth (boustrophedon) with odd letters
Roman and Byzantine periods use rounded 'lunate' forms: C for sigma, Є for epsilon, ω for omega
Byzantine icons use pairs of abbreviations with a bar above: IC XC, MP ΘY
scripts.onWhat: Painted vases (names beside figures, 'kalos' inscriptions), coins, stone stelae, gems, lead weights, papyri and mummy labels in Egypt, Byzantine seals, icons, crosses, ivories, enamels, mosaics.
scripts.infer: Greek letters mean the Greek-speaking world, which after Alexander stretches from Sicily to Afghanistan, so use the object type for place. Painted names on pottery are Archaic or Classical Greece (600-400 BCE). ΒΑΣΙΛΕΩΣ plus a name is Hellenistic (after 330 BCE). Lunate C-shaped sigma means Roman imperial or later. Greek with the extra letter Ϸ is Kushan (Bactria and Gandhara, 100-350 CE). Abbreviations with overbars and saints are Byzantine (after 500) or later Orthodox work.

confusables.how: Latin has no Σ, Π, Δ, Λ, Φ, Ω; watch Roman provincial coins that use Greek for eastern cities.
Coptic is Greek uncial plus six or seven extra letters (ϣ, ϥ, ϩ, ϫ, ϭ, ϯ) and comes from Egypt.
Early Cyrillic copies Greek uncial but adds Б, Ж, Ш, Ц, Ч, Ъ; on icons, Slavic letters mean Russia or the Balkans.
Etruscan uses archaic Greek letter shapes but runs right to left and comes from central Italy.
Archaic Greek letters still resemble Phoenician ones, but Greek has vowel letters and soon turns left to right.

styles.name: Archaic local alphabets
styles.where: Greek city-states, each with its own letter set
styles.look: Angular, uneven letters, right-to-left or boustrophedon; extra letters such as koppa (Ϙ, the badge of Corinth) and digamma. Sample shows the abbreviated Athenian coin legend and Corinth's koppa; real archaic shapes are rougher than this font.

styles.name: Classical and Hellenistic capitals
styles.where: Stone inscriptions and coins from Sicily to Bactria
styles.look: Even, geometric capitals, often in a strict grid (stoichedon); later with small serifs and broken-bar alpha.

styles.name: Roman-period and lunate forms
styles.where: Roman provincial coins, mummy portraits and labels, papyri
styles.look: Sample reads 'Emperor Caesar'. Rounded C for sigma, Є, ω; crowded legends around an imperial bust.

styles.name: Kushan Greek (Bactrian language)
styles.where: Kushan gold and copper coins, Bactria, Gandhara and north India
styles.look: 'King of kings, Kanishka the Kushan'. Blocky Greek with the added letter Ϸ (sh); deity names such as ΜΙΙΡΟ, ΟΗϷΟ, ΒΟΔΔΟ on the reverse.

styles.name: Byzantine uncial and icon abbreviations
styles.where: Icons, coins, crosses, ivories, enamels, mosaics
styles.look: 'Jesus Christ conquers' and 'Mother of God'. Letters with overbars, often stacked vertically beside a saint.

styles.name: Byzantine minuscule
styles.where: Manuscripts and lead seals
styles.look: 'Lord, help your servant', the standard seal invocation. Small joined letters with accents and breathings, hanging from a ruled line.

scripts.name: Egyptian hieroglyphs (with hieratic and demotic)
scripts.sampleMeaning: ḥtp-dj-nsw 'an offering which the king gives' (the funerary offering formula) + ankh, wedja, seneb 'life, prosperity, health'
look: Small recognisable pictures: birds, eyes, snakes, reeds, seated people, water ripples
Signs are grouped into neat invisible squares, in columns or rows, with no word spaces
Animals and people face the start of the line; right-to-left is the commonest direction
Royal names sit inside an oval rope ring (cartouche)
Often carved in sunk relief and painted, or written in black and red ink on papyrus
scripts.onWhat: Tomb and temple reliefs, stelae, coffins, statues, shabtis, scarabs, canopic jars, amulets, faience, papyri (Book of the Dead), ostraca, mummy bandages.
scripts.infer: Egypt or Nubia, and a 3,500-year range, so use the style. Tall crisp signs with spare layouts are Old or Middle Kingdom; elegant painted detail is New Kingdom (1550-1070 BCE); crowded, small, squat signs with many strange forms are Ptolemaic or Roman (after 332 BCE). Cartouches name the king. Cursive ink versions date too: hieratic for most of the period, demotic only after about 650 BCE. Garbled hieroglyphs on a non-Egyptian object suggest Phoenician, Roman or 19th-century Egyptomania.

confusables.how: Meroitic hieroglyphs borrow Egyptian shapes but use only 23 signs, face the opposite way, and separate words with dots.
Maya glyphs are rounded blocks with faces and bars-and-dots in a grid; Egyptian signs are separate, cleanly outlined pictures.
Indus signs are a short row of abstract marks above an animal on a small square seal.
Linear B signs are abstract line drawings scratched on clay, not pictures of animals and people.

styles.name: Hieratic
styles.where: Papyri, ostraca, linen, coffin texts; priests' cursive
styles.look: Hieroglyphs dissolved into quick brush ligatures, right to left, black with red headings. Not in Unicode.

styles.name: Demotic
styles.where: Legal and administrative papyri, ostraca, mummy labels; middle band of the Rosetta Stone
styles.look: Tiny, very cursive, comma-like strokes with long horizontal sweeps; looks nothing like pictures. Late Period, Ptolemaic or Roman.

styles.name: Ptolemaic and Roman hieroglyphs
styles.where: Temple walls (Edfu, Dendera, Philae), late stelae and coffins
styles.look: Crowded lines of small plump signs, many unusual ones, often in raised relief with rounded modelling.

scripts.dirNote: Unicode hieroglyphs display left to right; ancient texts more often ran right to left with the signs mirrored.

scripts.name: Cuneiform (Sumerian, Akkadian, Hittite, Elamite)
scripts.sampleMeaning: Sumerian d-en-lil2 lugal kur-kur-ra: 'Enlil, king of the lands'
look: Clusters of wedge-shaped (nail-like) impressions: horizontals, verticals, diagonals and angle hooks
Pressed into clay with a stylus, or cut into stone copying the wedge shape
Dense rows, often ruled into lines or boxed cases, no pictures
Tablets are pillow-shaped and fit in the hand; text often wraps around the edges
On cylinder seals: two or three boxed columns of signs beside a figured scene
scripts.onWhat: Clay tablets, cones, bricks and cylinders, cylinder seals, stone stelae and boundary stones (kudurru), statues, Assyrian palace reliefs, foundation figures, weights.
scripts.infer: Greater Mesopotamia and its neighbours, 3300 BCE to the 1st century CE. Sign shape narrows it: curvy pictographs or numbers on small tablets are Uruk period (3300-2900); neat signs in boxed cases on stone or cones are 3rd millennium Sumer; small crowded tablets are Old Babylonian (2000-1600) or Old Assyrian merchants at Kültepe in Anatolia; big clean wedges across the body of a relief figure are Neo-Assyrian (883-612); barrel cylinders and stamped bricks are Neo-Babylonian.

confusables.how: Old Persian has only about 40 simple signs and a slanted wedge as word divider; it appears on Achaemenid objects, often beside real cuneiform.
Ugaritic is a 30-letter alphabet of very simple wedge groups; signs are few-stroked and repeat often.
Linear B is drawn lines on clay, not pressed wedges.

styles.name: Proto-cuneiform
styles.where: Uruk and Jemdet Nasr tablets
styles.look: Drawn pictographs and round or D-shaped number impressions in boxes; not yet wedges.

styles.name: Sumerian monumental and Ur III
styles.where: Southern Mesopotamia: cones, statues, bricks, foundation tablets
styles.look: Complex, spacious signs in ruled cases. The web font follows this classic 3rd-millennium to Old Babylonian look.

styles.name: Old Babylonian and Old Assyrian cursive
styles.where: Letters, contracts, school tablets; merchant archives at Kültepe
styles.look: Small, slanted, tightly packed wedges on palm-sized tablets, sometimes in clay envelopes.

styles.name: Neo-Assyrian
styles.where: Palace reliefs of Nimrud, Khorsabad and Nineveh; library tablets; royal prisms
styles.look: Regular, squared signs made of clearly separated wedges; 'standard inscription' bands run across carved figures. No web font on Google Fonts.

styles.name: Neo- and Late Babylonian
styles.where: Babylon, Uruk: bricks, cylinders, astronomical tablets
styles.look: Archaising signs on royal bricks; very small leaning script on late scholarly tablets.

scripts.name: Japanese (kanji with kana)
scripts.sample: 色は匂へど 散りぬるを
scripts.sampleMeaning: 'Though the blossoms are fragrant, they scatter': opening of the Iroha poem
look: Chinese characters interrupted by much simpler, curvy signs (hiragana: の, は, し, を, る)
Angular simple signs (katakana: ノ, ハ, シ, ヲ) in glosses, Buddhist texts and modern labels
Brush-written kana flow together down the column in long unbroken threads
Vertical columns right to left; on prints, text sits in cartouches with a red seal
Poem cards and scrolls scatter thin wispy lines over decorated paper
scripts.onWhat: Hand scrolls and poem sheets, woodblock prints (title, signature, publisher and censor seals), sword tangs, lacquer boxes, ceramics, netsuke signatures, screens, sutras, armour.
scripts.infer: Any kana means Japan. Flowing hiragana poetry on decorated paper begins in the Heian period (after about 900); woodblock prints with signature cartouches and censor seals are Edo to Meiji (1680-1900); katakana with Western-style print is late 19th century onward. Text in characters only may still be Japanese: check for kana signatures, red artist seals and the object type.

confusables.how: Chinese text has no kana: every sign is a dense square character.
Hangul syllables are blocks built from circles and straight bars; kana are single loose strokes.
Vietnamese Nôm has no simple cursive signs between the characters.

styles.name: Hiragana (brush, with variant kana)
styles.sample: いろはにほへと ちりぬるを
styles.where: Waka poetry, tales, letters, print captions
styles.look: Soft looping signs joined down the column. Before 1900 many variant shapes (hentaigana) were used; this web font shows the modern set in a brush style.

styles.name: Katakana
styles.where: Glosses in Buddhist texts, official documents, modern loanwords
styles.look: Angular fragments of characters: short straight strokes and hooks.

styles.name: Kanji only (kanbun, man'yōgana)
styles.where: Sutras, official inscriptions, sword signatures, temple documents
styles.look: 'Namu Amida Butsu', the invocation of Amida Buddha. Pure characters, so the script alone cannot separate Japan from China.

styles.name: Edo print and theatre lettering
styles.where: Ukiyo-e title cartouches, kabuki programmes, shop signs
styles.look: Very thick, rounded, tightly packed brush characters filling their box.

scripts.name: Devanagari (Nagari)
scripts.sampleMeaning: 'Homage to Lord Ganesha', the usual opening of a manuscript
look: A continuous horizontal bar runs along the top of each word; letters hang beneath it
Many full-height vertical strokes on the right side of letters
Rounded bodies with loops; vowel marks above and below the line
Words separated by breaks in the headline; verses end with single or double vertical bars (। ॥)
Jain manuscripts: wide loose folios, bold black script, red circles marking string holes, gold on red or blue
scripts.onWhat: Paper and palm-leaf manuscripts (Jain Kalpasutra, Bhagavata Purana, Ragamala paintings), painting captions and versos, copper-plate grants, temple inscriptions, coins of north Indian states, bronzes.
scripts.infer: North, west or central India or Nepal, and after about 1000. Jain manuscripts in bold Nagari with small square paintings are Gujarat or Rajasthan, 14th-16th century. Captions above Rajput and Pahari paintings are 17th-19th century. In Mughal contexts it appears beside Persian nasta'liq. South India used other scripts, so Devanagari argues against the Dravidian south.

confusables.how: Bengali also has a headline but letters are more triangular and pointed, with a distinctive leftward hook on e/i vowel signs.
Gurmukhi has a headline but simpler, more open letters with few right-hand verticals.
Siddham has small wedge headmarks on each letter rather than a continuous bar and is written with a brush in East Asia.
Tibetan has a short head on each letter, a dot between syllables and long tails below; no word-long bar.

styles.name: Jain Nagari
styles.where: Western Indian Jain manuscripts
styles.look: Thick, square, evenly black letters; the e-vowel is written as a stroke before the consonant (pṛṣṭhamātrā).

styles.name: Ranjana and Newari scripts
styles.where: Nepal: Buddhist manuscripts, prayer wheels, metalwork; also Tibet as 'Lantsa'
styles.look: Ornamental relatives with thick curved hooks hanging from the headline, often in gold on dark blue paper.

scripts.name: Korean Hangul
scripts.sampleMeaning: 'The speech of our country differs from that of China': opening of the Hunminjeongeum (1446), modernised spelling
look: Syllable blocks assembled from a small set of geometric letters
Circles (ㅇ), small squares (ㅁ), right angles (ㄱ, ㄴ) and long straight bars with short ticks (ㅏ, ㅗ)
Much more open and airy than Chinese characters; the same parts repeat constantly
Traditionally vertical; early printed Hangul is rigidly geometric, later brush Hangul is softer
Often mixed with or glossing Chinese characters
scripts.onWhat: Printed and manuscript books, letters, late Joseon documents, some ceramics and embroidered textiles, folk paintings, 19th-20th century coins and banknotes.
scripts.infer: Korea, after 1446, and in practice mostly 18th century onward. Most Korean art objects (celadon, bronzes, paintings, epitaph tablets) carry Chinese characters only, so the absence of Hangul proves nothing.

confusables.how: Chinese characters are far denser and non-repeating; Hangul reuses a few circles and bars.
Kana are single flowing strokes with no circles-and-bars block structure.

scripts.name: Tibetan
scripts.sampleMeaning: Oṃ maṇi padme hūṃ, the mantra of Avalokiteshvara
look: Each letter hangs from its own short flat head; no continuous bar
A small dot (tsheg) after every syllable, vertical strokes (shad) at phrase ends
Letters stack vertically, with long pointed tails and hooks dropping below the line
Sharp, knife-cut look: thick horizontals, thin tapering descenders
Long narrow loose-leaf pages (pecha), often gold or silver ink on black or blue paper
scripts.onWhat: Thangka backs and borders, book covers and pecha leaves, prayer wheels, mani stones, bronzes (base inscriptions), ritual objects, tsakli cards, seals, amulet boxes.
scripts.infer: Tibetan Buddhist world: Tibet, the Himalaya, Mongolia, and Chinese imperial workshops of the Yuan, Ming and Qing. The script changes little over time, so date by the object. Tibetan beside Chinese, Manchu and Mongolian on one object is Qing court work (18th century).

confusables.how: Devanagari joins letters under one long bar and has no syllable dots.
Siddham letters are brush-written with wedge heads and appear singly as seed syllables in Japan and China.
'Phags-pa is Tibetan-derived but squared off and written in vertical columns.
Mongolian runs in vertical joined columns; Tibetan runs horizontally in separate syllables.

styles.name: Uchen ('with head')
styles.where: Printed books, inscriptions, formal manuscripts
styles.look: The block hand shown here.

styles.name: Umê ('headless') cursive
styles.where: Letters, documents, informal notes on thangka backs
styles.look: No top bars; slanted, quick, with very long sweeping tails.

styles.name: Lantsa (Ranjana)
styles.where: Mantras on prayer wheels, book title pages, temple beams
styles.look: Ornamental Indic script with heavy curved hooks, used for Sanskrit mantras.

scripts.name: Hebrew square script
scripts.sampleMeaning: 'Peace upon Israel', a common synagogue and funerary inscription
look: Separate square block letters, right to left, hanging from an imaginary top line
Thick horizontal strokes on top, thin verticals: a 'roofed' look
Many letters are open boxes (ב, כ, ד, ר, ה, ח, ם)
No joining; optional dots and dashes under letters for vowels
Torah-scroll letters carry tiny crowns (tagin) on top
scripts.onWhat: Torah scrolls and their ornaments (finials, shields, pointers), ketubbot (marriage contracts), Haggadot, Esther scrolls, Hanukkah lamps, Kiddush cups, tombstones, synagogue mosaics, incantation bowls, coins of the Jewish revolts (those use Paleo-Hebrew).
scripts.infer: A Jewish context, almost anywhere from Iraq to western Europe. Late antique mosaics and ossuaries are from the Levant; ink spirals inside clay bowls are Sasanian Mesopotamia (5th-7th century); illuminated manuscripts split into Sephardic (Spain to 1492, rounder letters) and Ashkenazic (Germany and France, Gothic-looking thick and thin); decorated ketubbot and silver are mostly 17th-19th century Italy, the Netherlands, Germany and Eastern Europe.

confusables.how: Imperial Aramaic is the ancestor: similar letters but more cursive, open-topped and slanted, on pre-Christian objects.
Syriac letters join into words; Hebrew letters stand apart.
Paleo-Hebrew on ancient seals and revolt coins is the Phoenician-type alphabet, not square script.
Kufic letters connect along a baseline; Hebrew letters are separate and hang from the top.

styles.name: Sephardic square
styles.where: Spain, Portugal, North Africa, later the Ottoman empire
styles.look: Rounded, even strokes of nearly uniform width; often with micrography (tiny text forming patterns).

styles.name: Ashkenazic square
styles.where: Germany, France, later Eastern Europe
styles.look: Strong contrast of thick horizontals and hairline verticals, influenced by Gothic quill writing.

styles.name: Aramaic incantation bowls
styles.where: Sasanian Mesopotamia
styles.look: Small informal square letters spiralling from the centre of a plain clay bowl to its rim.

scripts.name: Cyrillic (incl. Church Slavonic)
scripts.sampleMeaning: 'Lord, have mercy' (Church Slavonic)
look: Greek-looking capitals plus Б, Д, Ж, З, И, Л, Ц, Ч, Ш, Щ, Ъ, Ы, Я
Old texts: heavy upright uncial letters, little spacing, abbreviations under a wavy bar (titlo)
Icon labels: saints' names in a few stacked letters beside the head, IС ХС at Christ's halo
Ornamental 'vyaz' headings: tall letters squeezed and interlocked into a solid band
After 1708: civil type close to Latin print
scripts.onWhat: Icons, crosses, church plate, embroidered liturgical textiles, manuscripts, enamels, coins and seals, Russian silver and niello, lacquer boxes, Fabergé-era objects, porcelain marks.
scripts.infer: Orthodox Slavic lands: Russia, Ukraine, Bulgaria, Serbia (and Romania before 1860). Uncial 'ustav' is 10th-14th century; semi-uncial and vyaz headings are 15th-17th century; modern-looking civil letters are after Peter the Great's reform of 1708. On icons, Cyrillic labels separate Russian and Balkan work from Greek.

confusables.how: Greek has no Б, Ж, Ш, Ц, Ч, Я; Byzantine icons use Greek, Russian ones Cyrillic, though both keep IC XC and MP ΘY.
Glagolitic was made for the same language but its letters are loops and triangles unlike any Greek letter.
Latin lacks the mirrored-looking И and Я and the comb-shaped Ш.
Coptic is also Greek-based uncial but its extra letters (ϣ, ϥ, ϩ, ϯ) differ and it comes from Egypt.

styles.name: Ustav and poluustav (Church Slavonic)
styles.where: Gospel books, icons, liturgical objects
styles.look: Sample shows the icon abbreviations for 'Jesus Christ' and 'Mother of God'. Upright, wide, pen-made letters with archaic characters (Ѣ, Ѧ, Ѡ, Ѳ) and titlo abbreviation marks. No dedicated Church Slavonic web font used here.

styles.name: Vyaz (ornamental ligature script)
styles.where: Headings in manuscripts, icon borders, bells, silver, embroidery
styles.look: Tall narrow letters bound into a continuous decorative band. The web font is a modern display face in this spirit.

styles.name: Civil script
styles.where: Printed books, medals, coins, silver, porcelain of imperial Russia
styles.look: Rounded, Latin-like print letters; the hard sign Ъ at word ends means before 1918.

scripts.name: Ottoman hands (divani, tughra, ruq'ah)
scripts.sample: محمود خان بن عبد الحميد مظفر دائما
scripts.sampleMeaning: 'Mahmud Khan, son of Abdülhamid, ever victorious': the text woven into the tughra of Mahmud II
look: Tughra: the sultan's monogram, three tall shafts, two big loops to the left and a tail to the right
Divani: lines that rise toward the left, letters wound tightly together without gaps, bowl-shaped line ends
Gold and blue floral illumination filling the loops of a tughra
Ruq'ah: small, quick, short strokes with very few curls, an everyday 19th-century hand
Mirror-image and pictorial calligraphy (birds, ships, lions made of letters)
scripts.onWhat: Imperial decrees (firmans) headed by a tughra, coins, silver hallmarks, Iznik and Kütahya ceramics, sword blades and firearms, calligraphic panels (levha, hilye), tombstones with turbans, textiles.
scripts.infer: A tughra means the Ottoman sultanate, 15th century to 1922, and each sultan's is slightly different. Divani on a long paper scroll is an Ottoman chancery document, mostly 16th-19th century. Framed calligraphy panels and hilye are 17th-19th century Istanbul. Ottoman Turkish stopped using the Arabic script in 1928.

confusables.how: Nasta'liq words step down to the left with open space; divani lines climb to the left and are densely knotted.
Thuluth and naskh keep words separate on a level line; a tughra or divani text is a single interwoven mass.
Maghribi belongs to the far west and has wide round bowls, not stacked chancery ligatures.

styles.name: Tughra
styles.where: Head of firmans, coins, silver marks, buildings
styles.look: Calligraphic emblem: three verticals, two concentric ovals on the left, extended arm to the right. A unique Ottoman signal.

styles.name: Divani and celi divani
styles.where: Chancery documents
styles.look: Rounded, crowded, rising lines; celi divani fills every gap with dots and marks. No web font on Google Fonts.

styles.name: Ruq'ah (rık'a)
styles.sample: محمود خان بن عبد الحميد مظفر دائما
styles.where: Everyday handwriting, late documents, labels
styles.look: Short, clipped strokes; dots fused into dashes. The web font renders the tughra text in this hand, not as a tughra.

scripts.name: Arabic: Maghribi and Andalusi
scripts.sampleMeaning: 'There is no victor but God', the Nasrid motto repeated on the walls of the Alhambra
look: Round, generous bowls that swing far below the line; final letters end in open half-circles
Thin, even stroke from a pointed pen, less thick-thin contrast than eastern hands
Fa has a single dot below, qaf a single dot above
Qur'ans on squarish pages, brown ink with vowels in red, blue, green and yellow
Sudani (West African) variant is heavier and more angular, on loose leaves kept in leather wallets
scripts.onWhat: Qur'ans on parchment (later than in the east) and paper, Nasrid stucco and tiles, silk textiles, Hispano-Moresque lustreware, Almohad and Marinid coins (often square), West African Qur'an boards and amulets.
scripts.infer: The Islamic west: Morocco to Tunisia, Muslim Spain (until 1492), and from the 14th century the Sahel from Mauritania to northern Nigeria. Square silver coins are Almohad. The Nasrid motto is Granada, 13th-15th century. Parchment was used here centuries after the east switched to paper, so a parchment Qur'an in cursive is western.

confusables.how: Eastern naskh has compact bowls and dots fa above and qaf with two dots.
Kufic is fully angular; Maghribi grew out of it but is round below the line.
Nasta'liq hangs diagonally and belongs to Iran and India.

scripts.fontNote: No Maghribi face exists on Google Fonts; a naskh fallback shows the words but not the western letterforms.

scripts.name: Brahmi
scripts.sampleMeaning: Devānaṃpiya Piyadasi, 'Beloved of the Gods, of gracious mien': the title of Ashoka in his edicts

areas.label: Deccan & western India (cave inscriptions, Satavahana coins)
Tarim Basin (Kucha, Khotan; local Brahmi continues to about 900)

look: Simple geometric letters: circles, crosses, plus signs, hooks and angles, with no headline
Stick-figure look, well spaced, left to right
Small dashes attached to letters for vowels
Later (Kushan, Gupta) forms get small triangular heads and more curved, slanting strokes
On coins: tiny legend around a king, an animal, or symbols such as a hill, tree-in-railing or swastika
scripts.onWhat: Rock and pillar edicts, stupa railings and relic caskets, cave donations, coins (Indo-Greek reverses in the Ganges region, Satavahana, Kshatrapa, Gupta), seals and sealings, stone image pedestals (Mathura).
scripts.infer: India, from Ashoka (about 250 BCE) to the Gupta period, after which the script splits into regional descendants. Plain stick letters are Mauryan to Shunga (3rd-1st century BCE); letters with wedge heads on red sandstone image bases are Kushan Mathura (1st-3rd century CE); elegant curved letters on gold coins are Gupta (320-550). A coin with Greek on one side and Brahmi on the other is Indo-Greek, with Kharoshthi more usual in the north-west.

confusables.how: Kharoshthi runs right to left, is cursive with long slanted tails, and is confined to the north-west.
Siddham is the later, brush-like descendant with wedge heads and thick-thin strokes.
Devanagari has a continuous top bar; Brahmi has none.
Early Tamil-Brahmi cave inscriptions look the same; later Tamil letters are rounder and more complex.
On Indo-Greek and Kshatrapa coins the Greek side has A, Σ, Ω; the Brahmi side has circles and hooks.

styles.name: Ashokan / Mauryan
styles.where: Pillars and rocks across the subcontinent; early stupas (Sanchi, Bharhut)
styles.look: Plain monoline letters with no serifs. The web font shows this stage.

styles.name: Kushan and Kshatrapa
styles.where: Mathura sculpture bases, western Kshatrapa silver coins
styles.look: Small wedge or nail heads on each letter; more angular; letters start to lean.

styles.name: Gupta
styles.where: Gupta gold coins, Allahabad pillar, copper plates, seals
styles.look: Rounded, graceful letters with hooked tops and long curved vowel strokes; ancestor of Siddham and Nagari.

scripts.name: Kharoshthi
scripts.sampleMeaning: maharajasa rajatirajasa, 'of the great king, king of kings' (Indo-Scythian and Kushan coin legend in Gandhari Prakrit)
look: Right to left, cursive and slanted, unlike every other Indian script
Long tails curving down to the left; letters look like hooks, sickles and the number 7
No headline, uneven heights, thin pen or incised strokes
On coins: circular legend on the reverse, Greek on the obverse
On wooden tablets from the Tarim: ink lines on wedge-shaped double boards with clay seals
scripts.onWhat: Reverse of Indo-Greek, Indo-Scythian, Indo-Parthian and Kushan coins; Buddhist reliquaries; schist sculpture bases; birch-bark scrolls; wooden documents from Niya; pottery sherds.
scripts.infer: Almost a pin by itself: Gandhara and neighbouring Afghanistan, 3rd century BCE to 3rd century CE, or the southern Tarim oases in the 3rd-4th century. A bilingual Greek and Kharoshthi coin is Indo-Greek to early Kushan (about 180 BCE-130 CE); Kanishka dropped Kharoshthi from coins.

confusables.how: Brahmi runs left to right with upright geometric letters.
Kharoshthi descends from Aramaic and shares the right-to-left cursive look, but Aramaic has no attached vowel strokes and appears further west and earlier.
Pahlavi on Sasanian coins is also cursive right-to-left but appears beside a crowned bust and fire altar.
Sogdian is later, more connected, and found on paper in the northern Silk Road oases.

scripts.name: Coptic
scripts.sampleMeaning: ϩⲙ ⲡⲣⲁⲛ ⲙⲡⲛⲟⲩⲧⲉ, 'In the name of God', the opening formula of documents and epitaphs
look: Rounded Greek uncial capitals: ⲁ ⲃ ⲅ ⲇ ⲉ, with C-shaped sigma and ω-shaped omega
Extra non-Greek letters: ϣ (like a w with a tail), ϥ, ϩ (like a 2), ϫ, ϭ, ϯ (a cross-shaped ti)
Short horizontal strokes above letters or groups (supralinear strokes)
Thick, upright pen letters; later Bohairic hands are heavy with thin hairlines
No word spaces in early texts; crosses and staurograms at the start
scripts.onWhat: Limestone and pottery ostraca, papyrus and parchment codices, tombstones (stelae with crosses and niches), textiles with woven inscriptions, wall paintings, liturgical objects, magical texts.
scripts.infer: Christian Egypt, mainly 4th-12th century; ostraca and papyri cluster in the 6th-8th century around Thebes. After the 11th century Coptic is liturgical and often written beside Arabic, which signals a medieval or later date.

confusables.how: Greek lacks ϣ, ϥ, ϩ, ϫ, ϭ, ϯ and the supralinear strokes; without those letters a text from Egypt is simply Greek.
Old Cyrillic is also uncial but has Ж, Ш, Ъ and comes from the Slavic north.
Ethiopic letters are separate syllable signs with little flags and rings, not Greek shapes.

scripts.name: Phoenician, Punic and Paleo-Hebrew
scripts.sampleMeaning: ʿzbʿl mlk gbl, 'Azbaal, king of Byblos' (4th-century BCE coin legend)
look: 22 linear letters, right to left, no vowels, usually no word spaces
Angular strokes: zigzags (mem, shin), crosses (taw), circles (ayin), long-tailed letters leaning left
Letters look like tilted, mirrored versions of early Greek capitals
Punic versions become long-shanked and cursive; Neo-Punic is almost shorthand
Short texts: a name with 'belonging to' (l-) on seals and jar handles
scripts.onWhat: Stone stelae and sarcophagi, tophet markers, coins of Tyre, Sidon, Byblos and Carthage, seals and bullae, ivories, metal bowls, jar handles, ostraca.
scripts.infer: The Levantine coast from about 1000 BCE and the Phoenician colonies in Cyprus, North Africa, Sardinia, Sicily and Spain. Coins with this script start in the 5th century BCE. Tall thin Punic letters on a votive stela with a Tanit sign mean Carthage (to 146 BCE) or its Neo-Punic aftermath. The same alphabet on stamped jar handles and on coins of the Jewish revolts (66-70 and 132-135 CE) is Paleo-Hebrew from Judah.

confusables.how: Aramaic letters open at the top (bet, dalet, resh lose their closed heads) and look more cursive.
Archaic Greek uses similar shapes but adds vowels and Φ, Χ, Ψ and soon runs left to right.
Etruscan is found in Italy and has vowels and Greek-type letters such as 𐌈 and 𐌚.
South Arabian letters are tall, upright and strictly symmetrical, with word-divider bars.
Square Hebrew is a later Aramaic-derived script with boxy letters hanging from the top line.

styles.name: Paleo-Hebrew
styles.where: Judah and Israel: seals, jar handles, Siloam and Lachish texts, revolt coins
styles.look: lmlk ḥbrn, 'belonging to the king: Hebron', the stamp on royal Judean storage jars. Same letters as Phoenician with more curved, flourished tails.

styles.name: Punic and Neo-Punic
styles.where: Carthage, Tunisia, Algeria, Sardinia
styles.look: Letters with very long thin verticals; Neo-Punic reduces many letters to near-identical ticks.

scripts.name: Aramaic (Imperial, Palmyrene, Nabataean)
scripts.sampleMeaning: dryhwš mlkʾ, 'Darius the king'

areas.label: Iran to Afghanistan (Persepolis, Bactria, Ashoka's edicts)

look: Right-to-left consonant script, more cursive than Phoenician
Heads of letters open at the top; many letters reduced to hooks and short verticals
Imperial style: even, pen-written, with thick horizontals and thin verticals
Palmyrene: neat rounded letters carved beside the head of a funerary bust
Nabataean: tall, looping, with letters starting to join, the forerunner of Arabic
scripts.onWhat: Papyri and leather documents, ostraca, stone stelae, weights, seals, coins of Persian satraps, Assyrian tablets with ink dockets, Palmyrene funerary reliefs, Nabataean tomb facades and coins.
scripts.infer: The administrative script of the Assyrian, Babylonian and above all Persian empires (550-330 BCE), so it turns up from Egypt to Afghanistan. After Alexander it splits into local descendants: Palmyrene beside a limestone portrait bust is Palmyra, 1st-3rd century CE; Nabataean is Petra and north-west Arabia, 2nd century BCE-4th century CE; Hatran, Parthian and square Hebrew are cousins.

confusables.how: Phoenician keeps closed, angular letter heads; Aramaic opens and rounds them.
Square Hebrew is the formal book descendant: boxier, with every letter separate and upright.
Syriac joins letters into words; Palmyrene cursive is its close relative but usually carved letter by letter.
Parthian and Pahlavi derive from Aramaic and look similar; they accompany Iranian royal busts and fire altars.
Kharoshthi adds vowel strokes to the letters and is confined to Gandhara and the Tarim.

styles.name: Palmyrene
styles.where: Palmyra: funerary busts, honorific columns, tesserae; also soldiers' tombstones as far as Britain
styles.look: ṣlm … br … ḥbl, 'Image of … son of … alas!': the skeleton of a Palmyrene epitaph. Rounded monumental letters, often picked out in red.

styles.name: Nabataean
styles.where: Petra, Hegra, Bosra, Sinai graffiti; Nabataean silver and bronze coins
styles.look: šlm, 'peace', the commonest word in Nabataean graffiti. Tall, narrow, with ligatures and distinct final forms.

scripts.name: Syriac
scripts.sampleMeaning: b-šem abā w-brā, 'In the name of the Father and of the Son'
look: Right to left, letters joined along the baseline into short words
Low and wide: few tall strokes, many small loops and boxes
Dots above or below a letter distinguish d from r and mark plurals (two dots)
Estrangela is rounded-square and monumental; Serto is smaller and looped; East Syriac adds many vowel dots
Red headings and rows of four dots as punctuation in manuscripts
scripts.onWhat: Gospel books and lectionaries on parchment, mosaics and tombstones at Edessa, liturgical objects, magic bowls, Christian gravestones in Central Asia, the Xi'an stele.
scripts.infer: Syriac Christianity: south-east Turkey, Syria, Iraq, Iran, and missions along the Silk Road to China and to south India. Estrangela alone is 1st-8th century; Serto (West Syriac) appears from the 8th century; East Syriac vowel-dotted hands after the 7th. Cross-marked gravestones with Syriac from Kyrgyzstan are 13th-14th century.

confusables.how: Arabic has tall alif and lam strokes and deep bowls; Syriac stays low and compact.
Kufic stretches letters horizontally with rigid verticals; Estrangela is squarish and compact with dotted d and r.
Hebrew letters never join.
Sogdian derives from the same Aramaic stock and joins letters, but it is looser, with long tails, and is often written vertically.
Mongolian looks like Syriac turned on its side: a vertical spine with teeth.

styles.name: Estrangela
styles.where: Earliest inscriptions and manuscripts; later headings
styles.look: Rounded-square, open letters; the classical monumental form.

styles.name: Serto (West Syriac)
styles.where: Syrian Orthodox and Maronite manuscripts
styles.look: Smaller, rounder, more cursive; alaph is a simple upright stroke; small Greek-letter vowels above and below.

styles.name: Madnhaya (East Syriac)
styles.where: Church of the East: Iraq, Iran, Central Asia, India
styles.look: Close to Estrangela but with wedge-like strokes and vowel points made of dot pairs.

scripts.name: Pahlavi, Parthian and Avestan (Middle Iranian)
scripts.sampleMeaning: MLKʾn MLKʾ, read šāhān šāh, 'king of kings' (Sasanian coin and rock-relief title)
look: Right to left, cursive, with many letters looking alike (a row of hooks and loops)
On coins: a curving legend in front of and behind a crowned bust; fire altar with two attendants on the back
Inscriptional letters are separate; later 'Book Pahlavi' fuses them into ambiguous squiggles
On seals: a ring of script around a bust, animal or monogram on a domed stone
Avestan (manuscripts only) is a larger, clear, flowing alphabet with many more letters
scripts.onWhat: Sasanian silver drachms, stamp seals and clay bullae, silver plates and bowls (weight inscriptions on the rim underside), rock reliefs, ostraca; Parthian ostraca from Nisa and coins; Arab-Sasanian coins; Zoroastrian manuscripts.
scripts.infer: Iran and its empire. Parthian script appears on Arsacid coins from the 1st century CE; Pahlavi on a thin, wide silver coin with a tall crown is Sasanian (224-651), and the crown identifies the king. The same coin type with a short Arabic word in the margin is Arab-Sasanian (650s-700), and Tabaristan half-drachms run to about 790. Avestan and Book Pahlavi manuscripts are 13th century or later, from Iran or Parsi India.

confusables.how: Aramaic is the parent: clearer, more separate letters, earlier, and without Sasanian imagery.
Sogdian is also Aramaic-derived cursive but comes from Central Asia, on paper, coins with square holes, or with Turkic and Chinese neighbours.
Kufic has rigid tall verticals on a baseline; Pahlavi is a low string of curls.
Kharoshthi accompanies Greek on Gandharan coins, not Sasanian busts.
Syriac letters join neatly on a line and carry distinguishing dots.

styles.name: Inscriptional Parthian
styles.where: Arsacid coins, Nisa ostraca, early Sasanian trilingual reliefs
styles.look: MLKYN MLKʾ, 'king of kings' in Parthian spelling. Rounder, wider letters than Pahlavi.

styles.name: Inscriptional Pahlavi
styles.where: Sasanian coins, seals, silver, rock reliefs
styles.look: Separate, angular-cursive letters; legends get more cursive and careless after the 5th century.

styles.name: Book Pahlavi
styles.where: Late coins and seals, papyri, Zoroastrian books
styles.look: Letters fused together; a dozen shapes do the work of twenty sounds. Not in Unicode.

styles.name: Avestan
styles.where: Zoroastrian liturgical manuscripts, Iran (Yazd, Kerman) and Gujarat
styles.look: ahura mazdā, 'Lord Wisdom'. A 50-odd letter alphabet with full vowels, written in an even, rounded pen hand with dots separating words.

scripts.name: Ancient South Arabian (Musnad)
scripts.sampleMeaning: mlk sbʾ w-ḏ-rydn, 'king of Saba and dhu-Raydan' (Himyarite royal title)
look: Tall, upright, strictly geometric letters of equal height: circles on stems, rectangles, forks, zigzags
Monumental and symmetrical, like architectural ornament
Vertical bars between words
Right to left, or early on alternating direction line by line
Usually crisply carved in relief or sunk into alabaster or limestone; also cast in bronze
scripts.onWhat: Alabaster funerary stelae with faces, bronze dedicatory plaques and statues, stone building inscriptions, incense burners, coins imitating Athenian owls, seals; a cursive version on palm-leaf sticks.
scripts.infer: Ancient Yemen, roughly 8th century BCE to 6th century CE, with outposts in Ethiopia and north Arabia. Earlier inscriptions are severe and geometric; later Himyarite ones (1st-6th century CE) have flared, decorative letter ends. Alabaster heads and stelae with a name in these letters are Qatabanian or Sabaean, around 3rd century BCE-2nd century CE.

confusables.how: Ge'ez descends from it but runs left to right, is rounder, and marks vowels by small modifications of each letter.
Phoenician letters are slanted and irregular with long tails; South Arabian letters are upright and symmetrical.
Runes are also made of straight strokes but have no circles or rectangles and come from northern Europe.
Old Turkic is angular too but slanted and found in Mongolia and Siberia.

scripts.name: Etruscan and Old Italic
scripts.sampleMeaning: mi larθia, 'I [am] of Larth', the 'speaking object' ownership formula
look: Looks like archaic Greek capitals written right to left, so letters appear mirrored
No B, D, G or O; frequent 𐌈 (circle with cross or dot), 𐌚 (figure-8 f), 𐌑 (M-like sibilant)
Short texts, often running around the rim, foot or figure
Dots or colons between words in later inscriptions
Names beside mythological figures on mirrors
scripts.onWhat: Bronze mirrors, bucchero and painted pottery, cinerary urns and sarcophagi, tomb walls, gold tablets, bronze statuettes, coins, lead and bronze votives, boundary stones.
scripts.infer: Central Italy before Rome absorbed it. Seventh-century examples are on bucchero and gold; engraved bronze mirrors with labelled figures are 5th-3rd century BCE; alabaster and terracotta urns with a name along the lid are Hellenistic Volterra, Chiusi or Perugia (3rd-1st century BCE). Related alphabets write Oscan, Umbrian, Venetic and early Latin.

confusables.how: Greek has O, B, Δ and normally runs left to right after 500 BCE; an inscription on an imported Attic vase is Greek even if found in Etruria.
Latin runs left to right with B, D, G, O and familiar words.
Phoenician has no vowels and no Greek-type letters such as 𐌈 or 𐌚.
Runes probably derive from a north Italic alphabet and share angular shapes, but they are found in the Germanic north and are much later.

scripts.dirNote: Unicode Old Italic letters are stored left to right; mirror the line to imitate the usual right-to-left Etruscan direction.

scripts.name: Runes (Futhark)
scripts.sampleMeaning: horna tawido, 'made the horn' (end of the Gallehus gold horn inscription, about 400 CE)
look: Only straight strokes: verticals with diagonal branches, no curves and no horizontals
Made to be cut across wood grain, so letters look like twigs: ᚠ ᚢ ᚦ ᚱ ᚲ
On Viking stones the text runs inside a ribbon or serpent that loops around the face
Small dots or crosses between words
Short inscriptions on small objects: a name, 'made', 'owns', or the alphabet itself
scripts.onWhat: Rune stones, bracteates (thin gold pendants), brooches, weapons and scabbard fittings, combs, bone and wood sticks, whalebone caskets, coins of early England, church bells and fonts.
scripts.infer: The Germanic north. The 24-rune Elder Futhark on bracteates, brooches and weapons is about 150-750 CE (Denmark, Sweden, Norway, north Germany). The extended Anglo-Saxon futhorc is England and Frisia, 5th-11th century. The 16-rune Younger Futhark on memorial stones is the Viking Age, with most stones from 11th-century Sweden. Dotted medieval runes continue to about 1500.

confusables.how: Ogham is groups of plain notches along one edge line, not individual branching letters.
Old Turkic 'runes' look similar but come from Mongolia and Siberia, run right to left, and include curved and arrow-shaped signs.
Old Italic has round letters (𐌏-like theta, 𐌚) and comes from Italy centuries earlier.
Latin capitals include curves (B, C, D, O, S) and horizontals (E, F, T).

styles.name: Elder Futhark (24 runes)
styles.where: Scandinavia and the continent: bracteates, fibulae, spearheads, the oldest stones
styles.look: Includes ᛟ, ᛞ, ᛇ, ᛈ and ᚹ, which later disappear.

styles.name: Anglo-Saxon futhorc
styles.where: England and Frisia: the Franks Casket, Ruthwell Cross, coins, rings
styles.look: The first six runes, 'fuþorc'. Extra runes such as ᚩ, ᚪ, ᚫ, ᚣ; often mixed with Latin letters.

styles.name: Younger Futhark (16 runes)
styles.where: Viking Age Denmark, Norway and especially Sweden; Isle of Man, Rus trade routes
styles.look: raisti stain, 'raised the stone', the stock phrase of memorial stones. Fewer, simpler runes, set in serpent bands.

scripts.name: Armenian
scripts.sampleMeaning: 'Our Father who art in heaven' (Classical Armenian)
look: Rows of arches and hooks: many letters are built from one or two vertical strokes joined by a curve (Ա Ո Ս Ւ Ն Մ)
Looks like a string of u, n, m and h shapes with small flags
Capitals (erkatagir) are tall, rounded and monumental; later bolorgir is slanted and compact
Initials formed from birds, fish and knots in manuscripts
Carved in relief around the edges of cross-stones (khachkars)
scripts.onWhat: Illuminated Gospel books, khachkars, church facades, silver bindings and reliquaries, liturgical textiles, coins of Cilician Armenia, Kütahya ceramics, printed books.
scripts.infer: Armenians at home and in diaspora. The alphabet dates from about 405. Rounded erkatagir capitals are 5th-13th century; bolorgir minuscule dominates from the 13th. Lavish 13th-century Gospels are Cilician; 17th-century works are often New Julfa (Isfahan) or Constantinople; inscribed Kütahya pottery is 18th century.

confusables.how: Georgian letters are rounder and more varied, with loops and tails above and below the line, and no rows of arches.
Ethiopic letters are separate, squat syllable signs with small rings and flags.
Lower-case Armenian resembles u, n, h, but repeated in unfamiliar combinations with hooks.

styles.name: Erkatagir ('iron letters')
styles.where: Early Gospels, inscriptions, later headings
styles.look: 'Our Father'. Large upright uncial capitals with thick rounded strokes.

styles.name: Bolorgir (minuscule)
styles.where: Manuscripts from the Cilician period on; basis of printing
styles.look: Small, angular-slanted letters with short ascenders and descenders.

scripts.name: Georgian
scripts.sampleMeaning: 'Christ, have mercy' (a common inscription formula)
look: Rounded, curling letters with loops, hooks and tails; no capitals in the modern script
Old Asomtavruli inscriptions: even-height rounded capitals, many circles and semicircles
Nuskhuri church minuscule: angular, slanted, spiky
Mkhedruli (modern): very curvy with long ascenders and descenders, like a row of numerals 3, 6, 9
Abbreviations under a bar on icons
scripts.onWhat: Icons with repoussé silver and enamel, processional crosses, church inscriptions, manuscripts, coins of Georgian kings (sometimes bilingual with Arabic), metalwork.
scripts.infer: Georgia in the Caucasus. Asomtavruli alone is 5th-9th century and continues on icons and stone; Nuskhuri is the church book hand from the 9th century; Mkhedruli appears in the 11th century and takes over for secular use. Cloisonné enamel icons with Georgian labels are 10th-13th century.

confusables.how: Armenian is built from repeated arches and verticals; Georgian from circles and curls.
Burmese is also all circles but with Indic stacking and comes from Southeast Asia.
Glagolitic has loops and triangles too, but appears in Slavic church contexts in the Balkans and Croatia.

styles.name: Asomtavruli
styles.where: Stone inscriptions, early manuscripts, icon labels and titles
styles.look: 'kriste', Christ. Monumental rounded capitals of equal height.

styles.name: Nuskhuri
styles.where: Ecclesiastical manuscripts
styles.look: Same word in the angular, slanted church minuscule.

styles.name: Mkhedruli
styles.where: Royal charters, secular texts, modern use
styles.look: The rounded modern script.

scripts.name: Ge'ez (Ethiopic)
scripts.sampleMeaning: 'In the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit', the opening of most Ge'ez texts
look: Separate, upright, blocky signs of equal height, left to right
Each consonant has seven variants made by adding small rings, hooks and legs
Words separated by two stacked dots (፡); sections end with four dots (።)
Thick black pen strokes with red for holy names and headings
Parchment pages in two or three columns; scrolls with talismanic faces and eyes
scripts.onWhat: Parchment manuscripts (Gospels, Psalters, Miracles of Mary), healing scrolls, icons and triptychs, processional and hand crosses, Aksumite coins (also in Greek), stone inscriptions.
scripts.infer: Christian highland Ethiopia or Eritrea. Unvocalised and early vocalised forms are Aksumite (4th-7th century, coins and stelae). Nearly all manuscripts and icons in museums are 14th century or later; tall, slender letters suggest 14th-15th century, broader rounded ones the Gondar period (17th-18th century), and many healing scrolls are 19th century.

confusables.how: South Arabian is the angular, vowelless, right-to-left ancestor carved on stone in Yemen.
Armenian letters are narrower arches without the ring and flag vowel marks or two-dot word dividers.
Coptic is Greek-shaped; Ethiopic shapes are unrelated to Greek.

scripts.name: Linear B (and Linear A)
scripts.sampleMeaning: wa-na-ka po-ti-ni-ja: wanax 'king' and potnia 'mistress, lady', two titles from the palace tablets
look: Thin scratched line-signs on clay: crosses, tridents, little houses, figure-eights
Signs sit on ruled horizontal lines, left to right, with short vertical ticks between words
Mixed with pictorial commodity signs (horse heads, chariots, jars) and tally strokes for numbers
Tablets are long 'palm-leaf' strips or page-shaped slabs, grey or burnt orange
Also painted in a few large signs on stirrup jars
scripts.onWhat: Unbaked clay tablets preserved by fire, clay sealings and labels, painted transport stirrup jars.
scripts.infer: Mycenaean palace administration, about 1450-1200 BCE, at Knossos and on the Greek mainland. The similar-looking but undeciphered Linear A is Minoan Crete, about 1800-1450 BCE, and also appears on stone libation tables and gold or silver pins.

confusables.how: The Cypriot syllabary is a later relative with simpler, more angular signs, found on Cyprus and written right to left.
Cuneiform is impressed wedges, not drawn lines.
Hieroglyphs are detailed pictures; Linear B signs are abstract outlines.

scripts.name: Cypriot syllabary
scripts.sampleMeaning: pa-si-le-wo-se e-u-wa-ko-ro, 'of King Evagoras' (coin legend of Salamis, about 400 BCE, written in Greek)
look: About 55 simple angular signs: arrows, crosses, combs, Y and X shapes, small strokes
Usually right to left, with dots or short strokes between words
Looks like a cross between runes and tally marks
Often shallowly incised on local limestone
Sometimes beside the same text in Greek or Phoenician letters
scripts.onWhat: Limestone votive statues and their bases, tomb stelae, bronze bowls and tablets, coins of the Cypriot city-kingdoms, gold jewellery, pottery graffiti.
scripts.infer: Cyprus only, mostly 8th-3rd century BCE (the island kept its syllabary to write Greek until the Ptolemies imposed the alphabet). On a coin it means a Cypriot kingdom, 6th-4th century BCE.

confusables.how: Linear B is five centuries older, on clay tablets from Greece and Crete, with more elaborate signs.
Phoenician has only 22 letters with tails and no arrow or comb shapes; both occur on Cyprus.
Runes come from northern Europe a thousand years later.
Greek alphabet inscriptions on Cyprus become normal only after 300 BCE.

scripts.name: Old Persian cuneiform
scripts.sampleMeaning: Dārayavauš xšāyaθiya, 'Darius the king' (with the slanted word divider and the logogram for 'king')
look: Wedges, but far simpler and airier than Mesopotamian cuneiform: only 36 signs plus a few logograms
Each sign has two to five wedges; no crossing wedges
A single slanted wedge separates every word, giving a regular rhythm
Almost always part of a trilingual text, beside denser Elamite and Babylonian versions
Cut in stone or precious metal, never on everyday clay tablets
scripts.onWhat: Palace doorframes, column bases and reliefs, rock tombs, gold and silver foundation tablets, stone vases, cylinder seals, weights.
scripts.infer: Achaemenid Persian royal display, Darius I to Artaxerxes III (about 520-338 BCE). Finding it means the Persian court: Persepolis, Susa, Pasargadae, Hamadan, or royal gifts carried elsewhere.

confusables.how: Mesopotamian cuneiform has hundreds of denser signs with crossing wedges and no regular word divider.
Ugaritic is also a simple wedge alphabet but is on clay tablets from the Syrian coast 800 years earlier, with a small vertical wedge as divider.

scripts.name: Ugaritic alphabetic cuneiform
scripts.sampleMeaning: mlk ʾugrt, 'king of Ugarit' (with the word-divider wedge)
look: Wedge-impressed like cuneiform but with only 30 very simple letters
Many signs are one to three wedges in a row; the same few shapes recur constantly
A small vertical wedge divides words
Left to right on small clay tablets
Tablets look sparse and orderly compared with Akkadian ones
scripts.onWhat: Clay tablets (myths, rituals, letters, lists), a few inscribed bronze tools, ivories and seals.
scripts.infer: The city of Ugarit on the Syrian coast, 14th-13th century BCE, destroyed about 1185 BCE. A handful of examples come from elsewhere in the Levant and Cyprus.

confusables.how: Syllabic cuneiform packs many wedges into each complex sign; Ugaritic letters are minimal.
Old Persian is carved on stone monuments in Iran 800 years later and uses a slanted divider.

scripts.name: Meroitic
scripts.sampleMeaning: qore and kdke: 'ruler' and 'kandake' (queen mother), the two chief royal titles; words, not a sentence
look: Cursive form: small slanted strokes and hooks, right to left, resembling Egyptian demotic
Words separated by two or three stacked dots
Only 23 signs, so the same shapes recur far more often than in Egyptian
Hieroglyphic form: Egyptian-looking pictures but facing the opposite way and used alphabetically
Often on sandstone offering tables with a spout, around a scene of libation
scripts.onWhat: Sandstone offering tables and funerary stelae, temple and pyramid-chapel reliefs, royal stelae, ostraca, graffiti, bronze bowls.
scripts.infer: The kingdom of Kush with its capital at Meroe, about 2nd century BCE to 4th century CE. Egyptian-style art from Sudan with this script, rather than real Egyptian, is Meroitic period.

confusables.how: Egyptian uses hundreds of signs without dot dividers; Meroitic hieroglyphs use 23 and read toward the faces' backs.
Coptic and Old Nubian are Greek-based alphabets of Christian Nubia, after Meroe.
South Arabian is tall, geometric and carved in Yemen.

styles.name: Meroitic cursive
styles.where: Most inscriptions: stelae, offering tables, ostraca
styles.look: Demotic-like slanted strokes.

styles.name: Meroitic hieroglyphs
styles.where: Royal and temple monuments only
styles.look: 'qore' in the pictorial form: owls, eyes, lions and reeds used as single letters.

scripts.name: Khmer
scripts.sample: នមោ ពុទ្ធាយ
scripts.sampleMeaning: namo buddhāya, 'homage to the Buddha' (Pali, in Khmer letters)

areas.label: Angkorian empire (north-east Thailand, southern Laos, Mekong delta)
Central Thailand (Khom script for sacred texts)

look: Each letter wears a small notched 'hair' or crown on top
Tall, narrow letters with second consonants tucked underneath as subscripts
Angular and ornate in the slanted style; rounder in the upright 'mul' style used for titles
No spaces between words
Angkor stone inscriptions: beautifully regular rounded letters with curled flourishes above
scripts.onWhat: Sandstone stelae and temple door jambs, bronze ritual objects, palm-leaf manuscripts, folding paper books, yantra cloths and amulets, temple banners.
scripts.infer: Cambodia and the lands of the Angkor empire. Stone inscriptions with flourished rounded letters are Angkorian (9th-13th century) and may be in Sanskrit. On Thai manuscripts, amulets and yantras the same script ('Khom') is used for Pali well into the 20th century, so it does not exclude Thailand.

confusables.how: Thai letters have small loops at stroke ends and tone marks above but no 'hair' on top; Thai derives from Khmer.
Burmese is made of open circles with no crowns.
Javanese is more looping and wavy, with a row of repeated arch shapes, and comes from Indonesia.
Cham has similar Indic structure but looser, hooked letters and comes from the Vietnamese coast.

scripts.name: Thai and Lao
scripts.sample: กรุงศรีอยุธยา
scripts.sampleMeaning: Krung Si Ayutthaya, the name of the Ayutthaya kingdom and its capital
look: Upright letters, most beginning with a tiny loop like a pinhead
Tall narrow arches and hairpin shapes (ก ภ ถ ค ด); few horizontal strokes
Vowels and tone marks stacked above and below; no spaces between words
Lao is rounder and simpler with fewer letters and more curves
Manuscripts: long folding books (samut khoi) of cream or black paper with paintings
scripts.onWhat: Folding-book manuscripts, lacquer and gilt manuscript chests, bronze Buddha bases, stone inscriptions, Bencharong and Sawankhalok wares rarely, votive tablets, textiles, royal seals.
scripts.infer: Thailand or Laos, after the late 13th century (the Ram Khamhaeng inscription is dated 1292). Most inscribed objects in museums are Ayutthaya (1351-1767) or Bangkok period (after 1782). Rounded Tham letters mean Lan Na or Laos; sacred Pali text in Khmer-style 'Khom' letters is also common on Thai objects.

confusables.how: Khmer letters carry a notched crown on top instead of a starting loop.
Burmese letters are nearly full circles.
Sinhala is rounder and curlier still, with snail-shell spirals, and comes from Sri Lanka.

styles.name: Lao
styles.where: Laos and north-east Thailand
styles.look: Lan Xang, 'a million elephants', the Lao kingdom. Softer and rounder than Thai.

styles.name: Tham (Lanna / Lao Buddhist script)
styles.where: Palm-leaf manuscripts and Buddha bases in northern Thailand, Laos, Shan and Dai areas
styles.look: Very round, Mon- and Burmese-like letters with subscripts; used for religious texts.

styles.name: Khom Thai
styles.where: Thai Pali manuscripts, yantras, amulets
styles.look: Khmer letterforms written by Thai scribes: crowned letters, often slanted and angular.

scripts.name: Burmese (and Mon)
scripts.sample: နမော တဿ ဘဂဝတော
scripts.sampleMeaning: namo tassa bhagavato, 'Homage to him, the Blessed One' (Pali opening formula)
look: A chain of circles and part-circles, like bubbles or the letters C, O, U turned every way
Almost no straight lines in the everyday script
Small marks above and below; little spacing
Square 'tamarind-seed' ritual script: thick, blocky, dark-brown lacquer letters on gilded leaves
Palm-leaf pages with gilded and red-lacquered edges
scripts.onWhat: Kammavaca ordination manuscripts (lacquered cloth, ivory or metal leaves), palm-leaf books, folding parabaik books, stone inscriptions at Pagan, bronze bells, lacquer vessels, votive tablets.
scripts.infer: Burma. Stone inscriptions begin in the Pagan period (11th-13th century); nearly all portable inscribed objects (lacquer, Kammavaca, parabaik, silver) are 18th-19th century Konbaung or colonial period. Mon uses nearly the same letters.

confusables.how: Thai letters are upright hairpins with tiny loops, not full circles.
Sinhala is round too but with spirals and curls inside the letters; it comes from Sri Lanka.
Telugu and Kannada are rounded with a tick or 'check mark' on top of most letters.
Georgian is curly but alphabetic with tall ascenders and comes from the Caucasus.

styles.name: Round script
styles.sample: နမော တဿ ဘဂဝတော
styles.where: Palm leaf, paper, stone, lacquer
styles.look: The ordinary circular script.

styles.name: Square 'tamarind-seed' script (magyi-zi)
styles.where: Kammavaca ordination texts
styles.look: Bold square letters in thick black or brown lacquer on gold or red ground, six or so lines per leaf.

scripts.name: Kawi, Javanese and Balinese
scripts.sampleMeaning: hana caraka, data sawala: 'there were two messengers, they quarrelled', the first lines of the alphabet poem

areas.label: Sumatra & the Malay peninsula (Kawi, Old Malay)

look: Rows of rounded arches and waves: many letters look like m, n and w with curls
Even height, with small marks above and hanging subscript letters below
Old Javanese (Kawi) on stone and copper: neater, squarer, evenly spaced
Balinese: rounder and more open, scratched into palm leaf and blackened
Palm-leaf (lontar) strips threaded on a cord, sometimes with incised drawings
scripts.onWhat: Copper-plate charters, stone inscriptions and statue bases, gold rings and foil, bronze bells and zodiac beakers, lontar palm-leaf manuscripts, paper manuscripts from the courts of Yogyakarta and Surakarta, kris fittings, wayang-related texts.
scripts.infer: Indonesia. Kawi on stone, copper or gold is the Hindu-Buddhist period of central and east Java (8th-15th century). Paper manuscripts in Javanese script are mostly 18th-19th century court work. Incised palm leaves are usually Bali or Lombok, 18th-20th century.

confusables.how: Khmer letters are taller and crowned; Javanese is a low row of arches.
Burmese is circles; Javanese is waves and arches.
South Indian Pallava-Grantha is the ancestor: earliest Indonesian inscriptions (5th-7th century) look south Indian.
Cham comes from the Vietnamese coast and has more angular hooks.

styles.name: Kawi (Old Javanese)
styles.where: Java, Bali, Sumatra, Philippines: stone and copper
styles.look: The letters ha-na-ca-ra-ka in Kawi: a letter sequence, not an attested phrase.

styles.name: Balinese
styles.where: Bali and Lombok lontar
styles.look: ha-na-ca-ra-ka in Balinese: rounder, with generous curls.

scripts.name: Tamil
scripts.sampleMeaning: Oṃ namaśivāya, 'Om, homage to Shiva'
look: Squarish letters built from loops, right angles and long flat strokes
Fewer letters than other Indian scripts, no stacked conjuncts, so text looks open and even
Dots (pulli) above consonants; distinctive ம, ன, ண with multiple loops
Temple inscriptions run in long bands around stone plinths
Palm-leaf manuscripts with letters scratched and inked
scripts.onWhat: Temple wall and plinth inscriptions, copper-plate grants on a ring with a royal seal, bronze image pedestals, palm-leaf manuscripts, coins of the Cholas and Pandyas, hero stones.
scripts.infer: The Tamil south and northern Sri Lanka. Copper plates and temple inscriptions are mainly Pallava, Chola and Pandya (7th-13th century) and Vijayanagara-Nayaka (14th-18th). Before about 600 the same region used Tamil-Brahmi and then rounded Vatteluttu.

confusables.how: Grantha, used for Sanskrit in the same region, has more letters, rounder forms and stacked conjuncts.
Telugu and Kannada letters are round with a tick on top; Tamil is squarer with no tick.
Sinhala is all curls and spirals with no straight strokes.
Tamil-Brahmi cave inscriptions (3rd century BCE onward) are simple stick letters.

styles.name: Vatteluttu ('round script')
styles.where: Pandya country and Kerala: hero stones, copper plates
styles.look: Cursive, leaning, made of connected curves like a row of springs.

scripts.name: Telugu and Kannada
scripts.sampleMeaning: Oṃ namaḥ śivāya, 'Om, homage to Shiva' (Telugu script)
look: Round, bowl-shaped letters, most topped by a small tick or 'check mark' (talakattu)
No headline; letters sit separately like a row of pots with lids
Subscript consonants written below and to the right
Kannada ticks are flatter and letters slightly more angular; Telugu ticks are V-shaped
Medieval stone inscriptions are large, even and deeply cut, often below a relief panel
scripts.onWhat: Hero stones and temple inscriptions, copper plates, Vijayanagara and Hoysala coins, bronze lamps and ritual vessels, palm-leaf manuscripts, kalamkari textiles, Company-period paintings.
scripts.infer: The Deccan south: Karnataka, Andhra and Telangana. The two scripts were one 'Old Kannada-Telugu' script until about 1300-1500, so on older objects you cannot split them. Typical dynasties: Chalukya, Rashtrakuta, Hoysala, Kakatiya, Vijayanagara (1336-1565), Nayaka.

confusables.how: Sinhala is rounder still, with no ticks on top.
Burmese circles have no top ticks and no subscripts to the lower right.
Tamil is squarer with long flat strokes and no ticks.
Grantha and Malayalam are round but wider, with many double loops and no ticks.

styles.name: Kannada
styles.where: Karnataka
styles.look: The same mantra in Kannada letters.

scripts.name: Grantha and Malayalam
scripts.sampleMeaning: Oṃ namaḥ śivāya, 'Om, homage to Shiva' (Sanskrit in Grantha letters)
look: Wide, rounded letters with many double loops, like linked spectacles or pretzels
Stacked and ligatured consonant clusters for Sanskrit
Early Pallava forms are tall and florid with long curling tails
Malayalam: very round and wide, with large loops and few straight lines
