Often mixed with Tamil in the same inscription: Sanskrit words in Grantha
scripts.onWhat: Pallava and Chola temple inscriptions and copper plates, bronze pedestals, palm-leaf Sanskrit manuscripts, Kerala murals and manuscripts, the earliest stone inscriptions of Cambodia, Champa, Java, Borneo and the Malay peninsula.
scripts.infer: South India's script for Sanskrit, 5th century onward, and Malayalam in Kerala from about the 12th century. Its early Pallava form was carried overseas, so the oldest inscriptions of Southeast Asia (5th-8th century) are in it before local scripts (Khmer, Kawi, Cham, Mon) diverge.

confusables.how: Tamil has fewer, squarer letters and no stacked clusters.
Sinhala is closely similar and round, but found in Sri Lanka and with more spirals.
Telugu and Kannada carry a tick on most letters.
Khmer and other Southeast Asian scripts descend from Pallava-Grantha; by the 9th century they have their own crowns and shapes.

styles.name: Malayalam
styles.where: Kerala
styles.look: The same mantra in Malayalam letters.

scripts.name: Bengali-Assamese
scripts.sampleMeaning: Śrī śrī Durgā sahāy, 'Blessed Durga, be my help' (invocation at the head of documents)
look: Headline like Devanagari, but letters beneath are more triangular and pointed
Sharp wedge shapes and a hooked 'flag' vowel sign curling over the top left (ি, ে)
Fewer full-height right-hand verticals than Devanagari
Long, narrow palm-leaf or paper manuscripts with wooden painted covers
Signatures and captions on Kalighat paintings and Company-period drawings
scripts.onWhat: Palm-leaf and paper manuscripts with painted covers, copper plates, Pala-Sena stone image bases (in the ancestral script), coins of the Bengal sultans rarely and of Assam and Tripura, Kalighat paintings, kantha textiles.
scripts.infer: Eastern India and Bangladesh. The script separates from its Gaudi/proto-Bengali ancestor around the 11th-12th century; inscriptions on black stone Pala-period sculptures (8th-12th century) are in that ancestor. Most objects with clearly Bengali writing are 17th-19th century.

confusables.how: Devanagari letters are rounder with many full verticals; Bengali is angular with pointed loops.
Pala-period image inscriptions are in the Siddham-like ancestor of Bengali.
Tibetan has syllable dots and separate letter heads rather than a joined bar.

scripts.name: Sinhala
scripts.sampleMeaning: namo buddhāya, 'homage to the Buddha'
look: The roundest of all Indian scripts: nearly every letter is a curl, spiral or snail shell
No straight lines and no headline
Letters of even height with small hooks and loops attached
Palm-leaf (ola) manuscripts between painted or ivory covers
Medieval stone inscriptions on pillars and slabs, weathered and rounded
scripts.onWhat: Palm-leaf manuscripts and their covers, stone pillar inscriptions, copper plates, Kandyan ivory and metalwork, coins of medieval Lanka (which use Nagari), temple paintings.
scripts.infer: Sri Lanka. Earlier inscriptions (3rd century BCE-7th century CE) are Brahmi; the rounded Sinhala script develops from the 8th century. Most portable objects with Sinhala writing are Kandyan period (17th-19th century).

confusables.how: Burmese letters are plain open circles; Sinhala letters are curled and spiralled.
Telugu and Kannada have ticks on top.
Malayalam and Grantha are close relatives but wider with paired loops.
Tamil has straight strokes and right angles.

scripts.name: Gurmukhi
scripts.sampleMeaning: Ik Oankar, sati nāmu: 'One God, Truth is the Name' (opening of the Sikh Mul Mantar)
look: Headline script like Devanagari but simpler, squarer and more open
Many letters are plain boxes or hooks under the bar: ਸ ਮ ਹ ਗ ਪ
The ੴ symbol (Ik Oankar) at the start of texts
Few conjunct clusters, so lines look even and uncluttered
Often with floral illumination in Kashmiri style
scripts.onWhat: Guru Granth Sahib manuscripts and prayer books, Sikh portrait captions, coins of the Sikh empire (though most are in Persian), arms and armour, phulkari-related documents.
scripts.infer: The Sikh Punjab, from the 16th century; in museums mostly late 18th-19th century (the Sikh kingdom of Ranjit Singh, 1799-1849, and after).

confusables.how: Devanagari has more complex letters with right-hand verticals and stacked clusters.
Bengali is angular and pointed; Gurmukhi is boxy and plain.

scripts.name: Siddham (Siddhamatrika, 'bonji')
scripts.sampleMeaning: namo buddhāya, 'homage to the Buddha'
look: Indic letters written with a brush or broad pen: strong thick-thin contrast
Each letter has a small wedge or triangular head rather than a continuous bar
Angular, with sharp bends and tapering tails to the lower left
In East Asia: single large 'seed syllables' in a circle or on a lotus, standing for a deity
Rings of small letters around a central image on printed dharani sheets
scripts.onWhat: Indian stone and copper inscriptions of the 6th-10th century, clay sealings with the Buddhist creed, Pala bronzes; in East Asia mandalas, dharani prints, sutra scrolls, grave markers, sword blades, bells, reliquaries.
scripts.infer: Two different stories. In India it is the post-Gupta northern script (about 550-1100), for example the 'ye dharma' creed on clay sealings and image bases. In East Asia it is the frozen sacred script for Sanskrit mantras: on a Japanese object (after Kukai's return in 806) or a Chinese or Korean Buddhist one, usually alongside Chinese characters.

confusables.how: Devanagari joins letters under one bar and is not used in East Asia before modern times.
Tibetan has syllable dots and long stacked descenders; Siddham seed syllables stand alone.
Brahmi is the plain monoline ancestor without wedges or brush contrast.
Proto-Bengali grows out of eastern Siddham and keeps its wedges, adding a headline.

scripts.name: Mongolian (vertical script)
scripts.sampleMeaning: mongγol bičig, 'Mongolian script'

areas.label: Inner Mongolia & north China (Yuan to Qing)

look: Vertical columns read top to bottom, columns running left to right
Each word is a continuous spine with teeth, loops and tails projecting to the left and right
Words separated by gaps; word-final letters sweep away in long tails
Looks like Arabic or Syriac turned 90 degrees
On imperial objects it stands beside Chinese, Manchu and Tibetan
scripts.onWhat: Imperial edicts and letters, paiza (passport tablets), coins of the Ilkhans, Buddhist sutras (often gold on black), seals, stone stelae, Qing multilingual plaques and steles.
scripts.infer: Mongols, from Chinggis Khan's adoption of the Uyghur script (1204). Mongolian beside Arabic or Persian on a coin or decree is Ilkhanid Iran (1256-1353). Buddhist manuscripts and prints are 17th-19th century Mongolia or Beijing. Its parent, the Old Uyghur script (9th-14th century, Turfan and Dunhuang), looks nearly identical.

confusables.how: Manchu is the same vertical script with added dots and small circles beside letters and firmer, more regular strokes.
Sogdian is the ancestor: usually horizontal right-to-left, without the strong vertical spine.
Syriac runs horizontally right to left.
'Phags-pa is vertical too but made of separate squared letters, not a joined spine.
Tibetan is horizontal with syllable dots.

scripts.name: Manchu
scripts.sampleMeaning: boo ciowan, the mint mark of the Board of Revenue mint in Beijing on the back of Qing cash coins
look: Vertical joined script like Mongolian, columns left to right
Small dots and circles to the right of the spine distinguish sounds
More regular and upright than Mongolian, with crisp teeth
On coins: two vertical words flanking the square hole on the reverse
On plaques and seals: side by side with Chinese characters, Manchu on the left
scripts.onWhat: Qing cash coins (reverse), imperial seals, edicts and patents of nobility on brocade, palace name plaques, steles, book prints, jade books, archery and banner equipment.
scripts.infer: Qing dynasty, 1644-1912 (the script was created in 1599 and reformed in 1632). A Chinese-style cash coin with Chinese on the front and Manchu on the back is Qing; the two Manchu words name the mint. Bilingual Chinese-Manchu seals and plaques are imperial Beijing.

confusables.how: Mongolian lacks the systematic dots and circles and has more varied, sweeping tails.
'Phags-pa letters are separate squares stacked in a column, found on Yuan coins.
Seal-script Chinese on the same seal is made of separate symmetric characters, not a joined spine.

scripts.name: 'Phags-pa
scripts.sampleMeaning: mongxol tshi, 'Mongolian script' (the script's own name)

areas.label: Tibet (a derived seal script continues on Tibetan seals to the 1900s)

look: Square, angular letters stacked in vertical columns and joined by a line down the right side
Looks like Tibetan redrawn with only horizontal and vertical strokes
On coins: four blocky signs around a square hole
On seals: maze-like 'seal' version filling a square
Short texts: an imperial title, a reign name, a monk's or official's seal
scripts.onWhat: Yuan coins and paper money, paiza tablets, official seals, edict stelae, porcelain and lacquer marks rarely, banknote printing plates; later Tibetan and Mongolian seals.
scripts.infer: The Yuan dynasty: decreed in 1269 by Khubilai Khan and abandoned after 1368. On a Chinese-format coin or an iron or silver pass tablet it dates the object to within a century. A squared seal script derived from it survives on Tibetan seals into the 20th century.

confusables.how: Chinese seal script fills the square with one complex character; 'Phags-pa stacks a few simple repeating letters.
Tibetan is horizontal and curved with syllable dots.
Manchu is a flowing joined column with dots, on Qing coins.
Uyghur-Mongolian is cursive with tails; 'Phags-pa is blocky.

scripts.name: Tangut (Xi Xia); also Khitan and Jurchen
scripts.sampleMeaning: 'Great State of White and High', the Tangut name of the Western Xia empire, followed by a second, shorter form of the state name
look: Looks exactly like Chinese from a distance: square characters in columns
Up close no character is readable as Chinese, and each is denser, with more strokes
Many slanting strokes and repeated left-falling diagonals; few simple characters
Printed Buddhist texts with woodcut frontispieces; movable-type editions
Khitan (Liao, 10th-12th century) and Jurchen (Jin, 12th-13th century) scripts give the same 'almost Chinese' impression with simpler, sparser characters
scripts.onWhat: Printed and manuscript Buddhist sutras, coins, bronze seals with knob handles, stelae, paiza, banknotes; Khitan on epitaph tablets and bronze mirrors.
scripts.infer: The Tangut Xi Xia empire in north-west China (1038-1227), with late survivals to 1502. Most material comes from Khara-Khoto. Pseudo-Chinese characters on a north Chinese epitaph or mirror may instead be Khitan (Liao dynasty, 907-1125) or Jurchen (Jin dynasty, 1115-1234).

confusables.how: If you can find even common characters such as 大, 年, 天 it is Chinese; Tangut never contains them.
Nôm mixes real Chinese characters with new compounds; Tangut has no real Chinese characters at all.
Japanese has kana between characters.

scripts.name: Vietnamese Hán-Nôm
scripts.sample: 景興通寶 嗣德通寶
scripts.sampleMeaning: Cảnh Hưng thông bảo and Tự Đức thông bảo: two Vietnamese coin legends (18th and 19th century) written in ordinary Chinese characters. Invented Nôm characters are outside the coverage of Google web fonts, so none is shown.
look: Chinese-style square characters in vertical columns
Among ordinary Chinese characters, unfamiliar heavy compounds: two normal characters squeezed into one square
Most inscriptions on Vietnamese objects are plain literary Chinese with Vietnamese reign names
Coins: Chinese-format cash with Vietnamese era names (Cảnh Hưng, Gia Long, Minh Mạng, Tự Đức)
Blue-and-white ceramics with reign marks or poem inscriptions in loose brush characters
scripts.onWhat: Cash coins, bronze bells and drums, stelae, blue-and-white and 'bleu de Hue' ceramics, mother-of-pearl inlaid furniture, woodblock prints (Dong Ho), royal edicts, lacquer panels.
scripts.infer: Vietnam cannot usually be separated from China by script. Clues are Vietnamese reign names on coins and marks, invented Nôm characters, and the object type. Nôm writing flourishes from the 13th century to the early 20th; the Nguyen dynasty (1802-1945) accounts for most museum pieces.

confusables.how: Pure Chinese has no invented compounds; check reign names against Chinese ones.
Tangut contains no genuine Chinese characters.
Japanese adds kana.

scripts.fontNote: Nôm-specific characters (CJK Extension B and beyond) are not covered by Google Fonts CJK subsets.

scripts.name: Sogdian (and Old Uyghur)
scripts.sampleMeaning: βγy xwβw: 'lord, divine' and 'sovereign', two title words from Sogdian coins and documents; not a sentence
look: Cursive, right to left (later also in vertical columns), letters joined along a line
Low zigzag texture with long final tails sweeping left or down
Many letters hard to tell apart: a run of similar teeth and loops
Coins: Chinese-style cash with a square hole but cursive legend, or Sasanian-style busts with a Sogdian name
Ink on paper, wood or leather; also on silver vessels and textiles
scripts.onWhat: Paper letters and documents (Mount Mug, Dunhuang, Turfan), coins of Samarkand, Bukhara and Chach, silver bowls and ewers (ownership and weight inscriptions), wall paintings, textiles, funerary couches and epitaphs in China, steles in Mongolia.
scripts.infer: Sogdian merchants and their Silk Road network, 4th-10th century, from Samarkand to north China. A cash-shaped coin with cursive writing is 7th-8th century Sogdiana or Semirechye. The script passed to the Uyghurs (9th-14th century) and from them to the Mongols and Manchus.

confusables.how: Mongolian is the vertical descendant with a strong spine; Sogdian is mostly horizontal and looser.
Pahlavi comes with Sasanian royal imagery in Iran; many letter shapes overlap.
Syriac is neater, with dots distinguishing letters, in Christian contexts.
Kharoshthi is earlier and has attached vowel strokes; found on Kushan-era coins and wood tablets.
Arabic has tall alif-lam verticals and dots; Sogdian is a low ripple.

scripts.name: Old Turkic (Orkhon 'runes')
scripts.sampleMeaning: teŋri and türk: 'Heaven / God' and 'Türk', two key words of the Orkhon inscriptions; not a sentence
look: Angular rune-like letters made of straight strokes, with a few arcs and arrow shapes
Right to left, sometimes in vertical columns on stelae
Words separated by a colon (:)
About 40 letters; signs resemble ↑, >, D, Y, diamond and bow shapes
Cut on tall stone stelae, rock faces, or scratched on small metal objects
scripts.onWhat: Memorial stelae (often with a Chinese text on another face), rock inscriptions, silver vessels, bronze mirrors, belt fittings, coins of the Türgesh rarely, a few paper manuscripts.
scripts.infer: Turkic khaganates of the steppe: Second Türk and Uyghur empires in Mongolia (8th-9th century), Kyrgyz on the Yenisei (to 10th century). An unrelated-looking 'runic' text on a stele or silver cup from Mongolia or south Siberia is this, not Germanic.

confusables.how: Germanic runes run left to right, lack the arc and arrow signs and colon dividers, and come from northern Europe.
South Arabian is upright and symmetric with bar dividers, from Yemen.
Sogdian is cursive and joined; both can appear on the same Mongolian stele.

scripts.name: Glagolitic
scripts.sampleMeaning: glagolica, 'Glagolitic' (the script's name)
look: Letters built from small circles, triangles and loops attached to stems
Looks unlike Greek, Latin or Cyrillic: many symmetrical 'spectacle' and 'candelabra' shapes
Early round form hangs from the line; Croatian form is square and angular like blackletter
Red initials and ligatures in missals
Carved on stone tablets with interlace borders in Croatia
scripts.onWhat: Church manuscripts (missals, breviaries, Gospels), stone inscriptions and church lintels in Croatia, a few early printed books, graffiti in churches.
scripts.infer: The oldest Slavic alphabet, devised by Cyril about 863. Round Glagolitic is 9th-12th century Balkans and central Europe; the angular form is Croatian Catholic liturgy from the 12th century, with printing in 1483 and use to the 19th century.

confusables.how: Cyrillic letters are recognisably Greek-based; Glagolitic ones are not.
Georgian is curly but lacks the paired circles and triangles and comes from the Caucasus.
Ethiopic is blocky syllable signs with two-dot dividers.
Armenian is rows of arches.

scripts.name: Ogham
scripts.sampleMeaning: MAQI MUCOI, 'of the son of the kin-group of': the linking formula of ogham memorial stones

areas.label: Wales, Cornwall, Isle of Man & Scotland

look: Groups of one to five straight notches or strokes along a stem line
The stem is usually the corner edge of a standing stone; text reads bottom to top
Strokes to the left, to the right, across, or short notches on the edge
Looks like a tally or a barcode rather than letters
In Britain often paired with a Latin inscription on the same stone
scripts.onWhat: Standing memorial stones, a few bone, antler and metal objects, later manuscript margins.
scripts.infer: Early medieval Ireland and Irish-settled western Britain, 4th-7th century for most stones (Pictish examples in Scotland to the 9th).

confusables.how: Runes are individual letter shapes; ogham is counted strokes on a line.
Cuneiform wedges are impressed in clay in complex clusters, from the Near East.

scripts.name: Cham
scripts.sampleMeaning: Akhar Cam, 'Cham script' (the script's own name)
look: Indic structure: base letters with marks above, below and to the left
Loose hooked and looped letters, many resembling the numerals 2, 3 and 9 with tails
Stone inscriptions are neat and south-Indian looking; later manuscripts are slanted and wiry
Carved on sandstone stelae and door jambs of brick temple-towers
Often alongside Sanskrit in the same letters
scripts.onWhat: Sandstone stelae, temple pillars and pedestals (My Son, Po Nagar), metal vessels, later paper and palm-leaf manuscripts.
scripts.infer: The Cham kingdoms of central Vietnam. Stone inscriptions run from about the 4th to the 15th century; a sandstone sculpture or stele with this script is Champa, most often 7th-13th century. Manuscripts are 18th-20th century.

confusables.how: Khmer has crowned letters and tidy subscripts; Cham is looser and hook-shaped.
Javanese is a regular row of arches.
Early Cham inscriptions are in a Pallava-type script almost identical to south Indian Grantha.

scripts.name: Maya hieroglyphs
scripts.sampleMeaning: No Unicode encoding: describe by look

areas.label: Highland Guatemala, Copán & the Pacific slope

look: Rounded-square glyph blocks like pebbles or cushions, each packed with a main sign and smaller attached signs
Blocks arranged in a grid, read in paired columns, left to right and top to bottom
Many glyphs are profile heads of humans, gods, birds and jaguars; hands also common
Numbers as bars (five) and dots (one), often at the start with calendar signs in cartouches
Painted in fine black or red line on pottery; carved in relief on stone and jade
scripts.onWhat: Polychrome and codex-style cylinder vases (a band of glyphs under the rim), stone stelae, lintels, altars and panels, jade plaques and celts, shell and bone ornaments, stucco, bark-paper codices.
scripts.infer: The Maya area: southern Mexico, Guatemala, Belize, western Honduras. Almost all inscribed objects are Classic period (250-900 CE), and painted cylinder vases with a rim text are Late Classic (600-900). Long Count dates fix monuments to the day.

confusables.how: Central Mexican pictography is separate picture-signs and day names with dots, scattered in a scene, without the dense grid of compound blocks.
Egyptian signs are separate outlined pictures in rows; Maya glyphs are compact rounded compounds.
Bronze-script Chinese is linear and abstract; Maya blocks are plump and face-filled.

scripts.name: Central Mexican pictography (Aztec, Mixtec, Zapotec)
scripts.sampleMeaning: No Unicode encoding: describe by look
look: Picture-signs rather than text lines: a rabbit, reed, flint knife, house, each with a row of dots for a number 1-13
Year signs in square cartouches (Aztec) or with an interlaced A-O sign (Mixtec)
Place names drawn as a hill with an attached object; names shown as a sign linked to a figure by a line
Bright flat colours with firm black outlines in screenfold books on deerskin or bark paper
Speech shown as small curled scrolls from the mouth; footprints mark journeys
scripts.onWhat: Stone sculpture with date glyphs, carved boxes and calendar stones, screenfold codices and early colonial manuscripts and maps (lienzos), Mixtec gold, turquoise mosaic, carved bone, polychrome pottery; Zapotec urns and carved slabs with glyphs.
scripts.infer: Highland Mexico. Zapotec glyphs with bar-and-dot numbers at Monte Albán start about 500 BCE. Mixtec codex-style imagery is Postclassic Oaxaca (1200-1521). Aztec date glyphs on stone are about 1400-1521. Pictorial manuscripts with Spanish or Nahuatl glosses in Latin letters are early colonial (16th century).

confusables.how: Maya writing is dense grids of compound glyph blocks; Central Mexican signs are isolated pictures with dot numbers.
Colonial codices add alphabetic glosses in Latin script, which date them after 1521.

scripts.name: Indus script
scripts.sampleMeaning: No Unicode encoding: describe by look (undeciphered)
look: A single short row of about five abstract signs: fish shapes, jars, stick men, rakes, circles, strokes
Almost always above a profile animal (the one-horned 'unicorn', bull, elephant, rhinoceros) with a stand in front
On small square stamp seals of white-glazed steatite with a pierced boss on the back
Signs crisp and tiny, cut in intaglio so the impression reads right to left
Also on small copper tablets, pottery graffiti and moulded tablets
scripts.onWhat: Square steatite stamp seals, clay sealings, miniature tablets of faience and copper, pottery, bronze tools.
scripts.infer: The mature Harappan civilisation of Pakistan and north-west India, about 2600-1900 BCE. Nothing else looks like it; a few seals travelled to the Gulf and Mesopotamia.

confusables.how: Egyptian texts are long, with detailed pictures and cartouches; Indus texts are a handful of abstract signs on a seal.
Cuneiform is wedges; Mesopotamian seals are cylinders, not square stamps.
Brahmi appears over 1,500 years later and is a true alphabet in longer lines.

scripts.name: Cherokee syllabary
scripts.sampleMeaning: Tsalagi gawonihisdi, 'Cherokee language'
look: 85 signs, many borrowed from Latin capitals and numerals but with unrelated sounds (D, R, T, W, 4, Ꮞ)
Mixed with ornate invented letters with curls and serifs: Ꮳ Ꮂ Ꮹ Ꮿ
Reads like scrambled, decorated English capitals that spell nothing
Printed in a 19th-century serif typeface in newspapers and hymnals
No lower-case in historical material
scripts.onWhat: Printed newspapers (Cherokee Phoenix, from 1828), Bibles and hymnals, manuscripts and medicine books, signed baskets and carvings, treaties and broadsides.
scripts.infer: Cherokee Nation, after Sequoyah completed the syllabary in 1821: the Southeast until Removal (1838), then Oklahoma, with the Eastern Band in North Carolina.

confusables.how: Latin-looking letters appear, but the words are unpronounceable as English and include non-Latin shapes.
A few signs resemble Greek letters, but the object is 19th-century North American.

scripts.name: Rongorongo
scripts.sampleMeaning: No Unicode encoding: describe by look (undeciphered)
look: Rows of small outlined figures: bird-men, frigate birds, fish, plants, crescents, standing people with raised arms
Glyphs of even height packed tightly with no gaps
Every other line is upside down (reverse boustrophedon): you rotate the tablet at each line end
Finely incised with a shark tooth or obsidian flake on dark wood, lines running in shallow flutes
Carved on boards, a staff, and a few chest ornaments (reimiro)
scripts.onWhat: Wooden tablets, a chief's staff, reimiro pectorals, a birdman figure; only about two dozen authentic pieces exist.
scripts.infer: Easter Island, collected in the 1860s-1880s; the surviving pieces are probably 18th-19th century. Many tourist copies exist.

confusables.how: Indus signs are a short row on a stone seal with an animal.
Egyptian has columns, cartouches and many abstract signs; rongorongo is uniform little figures in inverted alternate lines.
Maya glyphs are compound blocks in a grid.
